lessons.title: What is Science? What is Physics?
lessons.notes_html:
Science is the study of natural phenomena and the laws governing them, built up by observation, experiment and reasoning.

Branches of Science

  • Physical sciences — Physics and Chemistry, the study of non-living things.
  • Biological sciences — Botany and Zoology, the study of living things.
  • Earth sciences — the study of the Earth and its surroundings.

Physics

Physics is the branch of science that deals with the study of matter, energy and their mutual interactions. It explains how and why things move, and the laws that govern heat, light, sound, electricity and magnetism.

Branches of Classical Physics

  • Mechanics — the study of motion and forces.
  • Heat (Thermodynamics) — the study of heat energy and its conversion into other forms of energy, or vice versa.
  • Optics — the study of light, its properties, its behaviour on reflection and refraction, and instruments based on it such as lenses, mirrors and microscopes.
  • Sound (Acoustics) — the study of sound waves, their production and properties.

lessons.title: Branches of Modern Physics
lessons.notes_html:
Modern Physics grew out of the study of atoms and the very fast and the very small. Its main branches named in this book are:

  • Atomic Physics — the structure and properties of atoms as a whole, especially the behaviour of electrons around the nucleus.
  • Nuclear Physics — the nucleus itself: its structure, radioactivity and the energy released in nuclear reactions.
  • Plasma Physics — the production and properties of the ionic state of matter (plasma).
  • Solid State Physics — the physical properties of solids, especially crystals and semiconductors; it explains how the arrangement of atoms in a solid gives it electrical, magnetic and thermal properties.
  • Semiconductor Physics — the study, design and use of devices based on the behaviour of electrons in semiconductors, such as transistors and computer chips.
  • Quantum Mechanics — the physics of very small particles and their wave-like behaviour.
  • Relativistic Mechanics — bodies moving at speeds comparable to the speed of light, where mass, length and time change with speed, as given by Einstein's theory of relativity.

Interdisciplinary Fields

  • Astrophysics — the properties and interaction of celestial objects; the physics of the universe.
  • Cosmology — the origin, evolution and structure of the Universe.
  • Geophysics — the internal structure of the Earth, earthquakes and its magnetism.
  • Biophysics — the laws of Physics applied to living organisms, for example how the eye forms images and how blood flows.
  • Medical Physics — Physics applied in medicine: imaging (X-rays, ultrasound, MRI), radiotherapy, and the safe use of radiation and laser instruments.
  • Computational Physics — solving physics problems with computers.

  • At home — electricity for lighting, and appliances such as refrigerators, fans and washing machines.

lessons.title: Hypothesis, Theory and Law
lessons.notes_html:
Hypothesis

A hypothesis is a tentative, testable explanation of an observed phenomenon. It is a statement put forward to be tested by experiments: if repeated tests support it, it may grow into a theory; if tests contradict it, it is rejected or changed.

Theory and Law

  • Theory — a well-tested explanation of a natural phenomenon. When a hypothesis is tested many times with positive results, it is given the name of theory; a theory is more certain than a hypothesis.
  • Law — a relation among different parameters of a phenomenon which has been found empirically true and applicable in all cases. A law states what happens, in a precise form.

Falsifiability of a Theory

Falsifiability (refutability) is the capacity of a statement, assumption, hypothesis or theory to be proven wrong. A scientific theory must make predictions that can be tested: if an experiment contradicts it, the theory must be given up or corrected. A claim that cannot be tested or disproved in any way is not scientific.

lessons.title: Physical and Non-Physical Quantities
lessons.notes_html:
A physical quantity is one that can be measured and expressed in terms of standard units, for example length, mass, time and temperature.

A non-physical quantity cannot be measured and cannot be expressed in standard units, for example love, hate, beauty and kindness.

Why Standard Units Matter

A standard unit makes measurements uniform, comparable and meaningful everywhere. Without agreed standard units, a measurement made in one place could not be understood or checked in another; trade, science and engineering all depend on everyone using the same units.

lessons.title: Base and Derived Quantities
lessons.notes_html:
• Base quantities — quantities in terms of which other physical quantities can be measured; they are independent of each other. Examples: length, mass and time.
  • Derived quantities — quantities derived from base quantities by multiplication or division of two or more base quantities. Examples: area, volume, speed and force.

Examples of Derived Quantities

  • Area — length × length
  • Volume — length × length × length
  • Speed — distance / time
  • Density — mass / volume
  • Force — mass × acceleration

lessons.title: Prefixes and Scientific Notation
lessons.notes_html:
Prefixes

Prefixes are used with SI units to write very large and very small measurements shortly.

PrefixSymbolValue
kilok103
centic10-2
millim10-3
microµ10-6
nanon10-9
  • One kilogram = 103 g
  • One nanometre = 10-9 m
  • 5 × 10-6 s = 5 microseconds
  • One cubic metre = 1000 dm3

Scientific Notation

In scientific notation a number is expressed as a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by some power of ten. It is a short way of writing very large or very small numbers.

  • 58000 m = 5.8 × 104 m
  • 300000000 m s-1 = 3 × 108 m s-1
  • 0.000000102 s = 1.02 × 10-7 s

Worked Example: Age in Seconds

The age of a girl studying in 9th class is 15 years. Convert her age into seconds and express it in scientific notation.

Step 1: 1 year = 365 days, so 15 years = 15 × 365 = 5475 days.

Step 2: 5475 days × 24 = 131,400 hours.

Step 3: 131,400 × 3600 = 473,040,000 s.

Step 4: In scientific notation, 473,040,000 = 4.7304 × 108 s.

Answer: 4.7304 × 108 s

lessons.title: Addition of Vectors: Head-to-Tail Rule
lessons.notes_html:
In the head-to-tail rule, vectors are added by placing the tail of the second vector at the head (arrow end) of the first vector. The resultant vector is then drawn from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last vector; it has the same effect as all the given vectors together.

For three vectors: draw the first vector, place the tail of the second at the head of the first, and the tail of the third at the head of the second, keeping each vector's length and direction unchanged. The resultant runs from the tail of the first vector to the head of the third.

Worked Example: Resultant of Two Forces

Two forces of magnitude 12 N and 5 N act on a body along the x-axis and the y-axis respectively. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant force.

Step 1: The two forces are perpendicular, so R2 = Fx2 + Fy2 = 122 + 52 = 144 + 25 = 169.

Step 2: R = 13 N.

Step 3: Direction: tan θ = Fy / Fx = 5 / 12 = 0.4167, so θ = 22.6 degrees with the x-axis.

Answer: 13 N at 22.6 degrees to the x-axis

lessons.title: Measuring Length: Metre Rule, Tape and Vernier Callipers
lessons.notes_html:
• Metre rule — measures length in centimetres and millimetres; its least count is 1 mm.
  • Measuring tape — used for longer lengths, such as the length of a room or a playground.
  • Vernier callipers — measures small lengths, and the internal and external diameters of objects, much more accurately.

Least Count of Vernier Callipers

Least count = 0.01 cm

  • The least count is the smallest length the instrument can measure: 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm.
  • Every Vernier reading is recorded correct to this least count: a diameter recorded as 1.032 cm can only be trusted as 1.03 cm.

Zero Error

Zero error is the reading an instrument shows when it should read zero — for example, when the jaws of Vernier callipers are fully closed. If the zero reading is not zero, that amount must be subtracted from (or added to) every measurement to get the correct value.

Worked Example: A Vernier Reading

Step 1: Main-scale reading = 4.3 cm.

Step 2: The Vernier division that coincides with a main-scale division adds 0.05 cm.

Step 3: Reading = main scale + Vernier coincidence × least count = 4.3 + 0.05 = 4.35 cm.

Answer: 4.35 cm

lessons.title: Micrometer Screw Gauge
lessons.notes_html:
The micrometer screw gauge measures very small lengths, such as the diameter of a thin metallic wire. It is the most suitable instrument for such fine measurements.

Least Count of Screw Gauge

Least count = 0.001 cm

  • The least count of a screw gauge is 0.01 mm = 0.001 cm.
  • It is ten times finer than a Vernier callipers, which is why a screw gauge is used for very thin objects such as wires.
  • The pitch of the screw is the distance the spindle moves forward in one complete rotation; least count = pitch / number of divisions on the circular scale.
  • Zero error is checked by closing the spindle against the anvil: the reading should be zero.

Worked Example: A Screw Gauge Reading

Step 1: Read the main scale on the sleeve.

Step 2: Read the circular-scale division that coincides with the reference line, and multiply it by the least count (0.01 mm).

Step 3: Add the two readings (and correct for zero error if any). For the figure in the book, the reading so obtained is 5.78 mm.

Answer: 5.78 mm

lessons.title: Measurement of Volume and Time
lessons.notes_html:
Volume by Measuring Cylinder

Pour water into a graduated measuring cylinder and note its initial level. Tie the solid with a thread and lower it fully into the water; note the new, higher level. The rise in the water level equals the volume of the solid, because the solid displaces its own volume of water.

Volume of solid = final reading - initial reading

Measurement of Time

  • Mechanical stopwatch — can measure a time interval up to a minimum of 0.1 s.
  • Digital stopwatch — also measures to a minimum of 0.1 s, and is read directly from its display.

Worked Example: Volume of a Sphere

The radius of a metallic sphere is 2.35 cm. Calculate its volume up to a reasonable number of significant figures.

Step 1: V = 4/3 π r3 = 4/3 × 3.14 × (2.35)3.

Step 2: (2.35)3 = 12.977.

Step 3: V = 4.1888 × 12.977 = 54.36 cm3.

Step 4: The radius has three significant figures, so round the answer to three significant figures.

Answer: 54.4 cm3

lessons.notes_html:
• Systematic error — repeats in a measurement with the same magnitude and the same sign, for example the zero error of an instrument or a wrongly calibrated scale. It can be found and corrected.
  • Random error — repeats with different magnitude and sign under the same experimental conditions, for example slight changes in the observer's eye position (parallax) or small vibrations. It is reduced by taking several readings and averaging them.

lessons.title: Significant Figures and Rounding
lessons.notes_html:
Significant figures are the accurately known digits plus the first uncertain (doubtful) digit in a measurement.

Rules for Counting Significant Figures

  • All non-zero digits are significant: 23.4506 has 6 significant figures.
  • Zeros between non-zero digits are significant: 2003 has 4.
  • Leading zeros are not significant: 0.0006032 has 4 significant figures (6, 0, 3, 2).
  • A trailing zero after a decimal point is significant: 15.30 has 4.
  • In scientific notation only the coefficient counts: 5.98 × 1024 has 3.

Worked Example: Counting Significant Figures

State the number of significant figures in: (a) 234567 m (b) 2003 kg (c) 0.000529 s (d) 5.98 × 1024 kg (e) 15.30 J

Step 1: (a) All six digits are significant: 6.

Step 2: (b) The zeros between non-zero digits count: 4.

Step 3: (c) Leading zeros do not count; 5, 2, 9 count: 3.

Step 4: (d) The coefficient 5.98 has 3; the power of ten adds none.

Step 5: (e) The trailing zero after the decimal point counts: 4.

Answer: (a) 6, (b) 4, (c) 3, (d) 3, (e) 4

Rounding Off

To round to three significant figures, keep three figures and round on the fourth digit: round down if it is less than 5, round up if it is 5 or more. For example, 8.724 becomes 8.72 and 8.737 becomes 8.74.

The final answer of a calculation is rounded to the number of significant figures of the least precise measurement used in it.

Key Points

  • SI has seven base units; all other units are derived from them.
  • A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has magnitude and direction.
  • Least count: Vernier callipers 0.01 cm; screw gauge 0.001 cm.
  • Systematic errors repeat with the same sign; random errors change sign and size.
  • Significant figures = all accurately known digits + one doubtful digit.

lessons.title: Rest and Motion; Types of Motion
lessons.notes_html:
Kinematics is the branch of Mechanics that deals with the study of motion of bodies without reference to the forces that cause the motion. It describes motion in terms of displacement, velocity, acceleration and time.

Rest and Motion

  • Rest — a body does not change its position with respect to its surroundings with time, for example a book lying on a table.
  • Motion — a body changes its position with respect to its surroundings with time, for example a moving car or a flying bird.

Types of Motion

  • Translatory motion — the body moves along a line without rotation. It is of three kinds: linear motion (along a straight line, e.g. a car on a straight road), circular motion (along a circular path, e.g. a stone whirled on a string) and random motion (no fixed path or direction, e.g. the flight of a butterfly).
  • Rotatory motion — the body spins about a fixed axis while its particles move in circles around that axis, e.g. the spinning of the Earth and the blades of an electric fan.
  • Vibratory motion — to-and-fro motion about a mean (rest) position, repeated after equal intervals of time, e.g. the pendulum of a clock, a vibrating guitar string and a swing.

lessons.title: Distance and Displacement
lessons.notes_html:
• Distance — the total length of the path actually travelled by a body. It is a scalar quantity and is always positive.
  • Displacement — the shortest distance from the initial point to the final point, in a stated direction. It is a vector quantity and can be positive, negative or zero.

Worked Example: Distance and Displacement

A girl travels a distance of 20 m towards West, then 30 m towards North and finally 20 m towards East. Calculate (a) the total distance travelled, (b) the resultant displacement.

Step 1: Total distance = 20 + 30 + 20 = 70 m.

Step 2: The 20 m West and the 20 m East cancel each other, leaving only the 30 m North.

Answer: (a) 70 m, (b) 30 m towards North

mcqs.q: Distance is defined as:
options: The shortest distance from initial to final point
The total length of the path actually travelled
mcqs.why: Distance is the total length of the path actually travelled by a body; it is a scalar quantity and is always positive.

mcqs.q: Displacement is a:
mcqs.why: Displacement is the shortest distance from the initial point to the final point in a stated direction, so it is a vector and can be positive, negative or zero.

mcqs.why: Total distance = 20 + 30 + 20 = 70 m, adding the lengths of all three parts of the path actually travelled.

mcqs.q: For the girl travelling 20 m West, 30 m North and 20 m East, the resultant displacement is:
mcqs.why: The 20 m West and 20 m East cancel each other, leaving only the 30 m North, so the resultant displacement is 30 m towards North.

mcqs.q: Which statement about distance is correct?
mcqs.why: Distance is a scalar quantity and is always positive, unlike displacement which is a vector and can be positive, negative or zero.

mcqs.q: Displacement can be:
mcqs.why: Displacement is a vector quantity, the shortest distance in a stated direction, and the notes state it can be positive, negative or zero.

mcqs.q: If a body returns to its starting point after a journey, its displacement is:
mcqs.why: Displacement is the shortest distance from initial to final point; if both points are the same, that distance is zero even though distance travelled is not.

mcqs.q: Distance is a scalar quantity because it has:
mcqs.why: A scalar is specified by magnitude only; distance is the total path length with no stated direction, so it is a scalar quantity.

mcqs.why: By definition displacement is the shortest distance from the initial point to the final point in a stated direction, and it is a vector quantity.

lessons.title: Speed and Velocity
lessons.notes_html:
Speed

Speed is the distance covered by a body in unit time. It is a scalar quantity.

Speed = distance / time

  • Uniform speed — the body covers equal distances in equal intervals of time, however small the intervals may be.
  • Average speed — total distance / total time.
  • Instantaneous speed — the speed of the body at a particular instant.

Velocity

Velocity is the time rate of change of displacement: displacement per unit time in a stated direction. It is a vector quantity.

Velocity = displacement / time

  • Uniform velocity — equal displacements in equal intervals of time.
  • Non-uniform velocity — unequal displacements, or a changing direction.
  • Average velocity — total displacement / total time.

Worked Example: Average Speed

A car travels 100 metres in 5 seconds. What is its average speed?

Step 1: Average speed = total distance / total time.

Step 2: Average speed = 100 / 5 = 20 m s-1.

Answer: 20 m s-1

Worked Example: Changing Units of Speed

Step 1: To change km h-1 into m s-1, divide by 3.6: 90 / 3.6 = 25 m s-1.

Step 2: To change m s-1 into km h-1, multiply by 3.6: 30 × 3.6 = 108 km h-1.

Answer: 90 km h-1 is 25 m s-1; 30 m s-1 is 108 km h-1

mcqs.q: Speed is defined as:
options: Change in velocity per unit time
mcqs.why: Speed is the distance covered by a body in unit time, Speed = distance / time, and it is a scalar quantity as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: A car travels 100 m in 5 s. What is its average speed?
mcqs.why: Average speed = total distance / total time = 100 / 5 = 20 m/s, exactly as worked in the notes example.

mcqs.why: To change km/h into m/s divide by 3.6: 90 / 3.6 = 25 m/s, as shown in the notes worked example on changing units.

mcqs.q: 30 m/s is equal to how many km/h?
mcqs.why: To change m/s into km/h multiply by 3.6: 30 x 3.6 = 108 km/h, as shown in the notes worked example.

mcqs.q: Velocity is:
options: The time rate of change of displacement
mcqs.why: Velocity is the time rate of change of displacement, displacement per unit time in a stated direction, and it is a vector quantity.

Equal displacements only in one direction
mcqs.why: Uniform speed means the body covers equal distances in equal intervals of time, however small the intervals may be.

mcqs.why: Average speed = total distance / total time, while average velocity = total displacement / total time, as defined in the notes.

mcqs.q: The speed of a body at a particular instant is called:
mcqs.why: Instantaneous speed is the speed of the body at a particular instant, distinct from average speed over a whole journey.

mcqs.why: Uniform velocity means equal displacements in equal intervals of time; unequal displacements or a changing direction give non-uniform velocity.

mcqs.q: Which quantity is a vector?
mcqs.why: Velocity is displacement per unit time in a stated direction, so it is a vector quantity, whereas speed is a scalar quantity.

lessons.title: Acceleration
lessons.notes_html:
Acceleration is the time rate of change of velocity of a body. It is a vector quantity, measured in metre per second squared (m s-2). It is positive when velocity increases and negative (retardation) when velocity decreases.

Acceleration = change in velocity / time

  • Uniform acceleration — velocity changes by equal amounts in equal intervals of time.
  • Non-uniform acceleration — velocity changes by unequal amounts in equal intervals of time.

Worked Example: Acceleration of a Car

A car accelerates from 5 m s-1 to 25 m s-1 in 10 seconds. What is its acceleration?

Step 1: a = (vf - vi) / t

Step 2: a = (25 - 5) / 10 = 20 / 10 = 2 m s-2.

Answer: 2 m s-2

Worked Example: Retardation

A car moving with a velocity of 72 km h-1 is brought to rest in 10 s. Calculate the retardation of the car.

Step 1: Convert: 72 km h-1 = 72 / 3.6 = 20 m s-1.

Step 2: a = (0 - 20) / 10 = -2 m s-2. The negative sign shows retardation.

Answer: retardation of 2 m s-2

lessons.title: Motion Graphs
lessons.notes_html:
Distance-Time Graph

  • A horizontal line parallel to the time axis means the distance does not change: the object is at rest.
  • An inclined straight line means uniform speed; the slope of the line gives the speed.
  • A curved line means variable (non-uniform) speed.

Speed-Time Graph

  • For constant acceleration the speed-time graph is a straight line inclined to the time axis (through the origin if the body starts from rest).
  • The slope of the speed-time graph gives the acceleration.
  • The area under the speed-time graph gives the distance covered (displacement for a velocity-time graph).

Worked Example: Reading a Speed-Time Graph

The graph above is the speed-time graph of a motor cycle: its speed rises from 0 to 40 m s-1 in the first 20 s, stays at 40 m s-1 from 20 s to 40 s, then falls to 0 in the last 10 s.

Step 1: Maximum speed = 40 m s-1, and it stays at this speed for 40 - 20 = 20 s.

Step 2: Speed gained in the first 20 s = 40 m s-1, so it gains 40 / 20 = 2 m s-1 every second: acceleration = 2 m s-2.

Step 3: Retardation in the last 10 s = (0 - 40) / 10 = -4 m s-2.

Answer: maximum speed 40 m s-1; acceleration 2 m s-2; retardation 4 m s-2

lessons.title: Equations of Motion
lessons.notes_html:
For motion with uniform acceleration, three equations connect initial velocity vi, final velocity vf, acceleration a, time t and distance S. They are derived from the speed-time graph.

First Equation of Motion

vf = vi + at

  • The slope of the speed-time graph is a = (vf - vi) / t, which gives this equation.

Second Equation of Motion

S = vi t + 1/2 a t2

  • The distance covered is the area under the speed-time graph (a trapezium), which gives this equation.

Third Equation of Motion

2aS = vf2 - vi2

  • Putting t = (vf - vi) / a from the first equation into the second gives this equation.

Worked Example: Take-Off of an Aeroplane

An aeroplane must acquire a velocity of 71 m s-1 for take-off. If the runway is 1.0 km long, what must be the acceleration of the aeroplane?

Step 1: Use 2aS = vf2 - vi2 with vi = 0 and S = 1000 m.

Step 2: a = 712 / (2 × 1000) = 5041 / 2000 = 2.52 m s-2.

Answer: 2.52 m s-2

Worked Example: Braking Distance

A racing car is moving at 180 km h-1. Brakes are applied and a negative acceleration of 10 m s-2 is produced. Calculate the distance covered before coming to rest.

Step 1: Convert: 180 km h-1 = 180 / 3.6 = 50 m s-1.

Step 2: S = (0 - 502) / (2 × -10) = (-2500) / (-20) = 125 m.

Answer: 125 m

lessons.title: Motion under Gravity and the Speed Limit
lessons.notes_html:
Acceleration due to gravity is the uniform acceleration of a freely falling body under the Earth's gravitational pull, when air resistance is ignored. Its value near the Earth's surface is:

g = 9.8 m s-2

  • It is directed towards the centre of the Earth.
  • All bodies fall with the same acceleration: two balls of different masses dropped from a tower reach the ground at the same time.
  • A ball dropped freely covers 4.9 m in the first second.
  • For a body thrown upwards, the velocity at the highest point is zero.
  • The equations of motion apply with a replaced by g (negative for upward motion).

Worked Example: Ball Thrown Upwards

A ball is thrown up vertically with a speed of 49 m s-1. (a) How long does it take to reach its highest point? (b) How high does the ball rise? Take g = 9.8 m s-2.

Step 1: At the highest point vf = 0, so t = (vf - vi) / (-g) = (0 - 49) / (-9.8) = 5 s.

Step 2: h = vi2 / (2g) = 492 / (2 × 9.8) = 2401 / 19.6 = 122.5 m.

Answer: (a) 5 s, (b) 122.5 m

The Universal Speed Limit

The speed limit for any object in the universe is the speed of light in vacuum:

c = 3 × 108 m s-1

  • According to relativity, no material object can reach or exceed this speed.

Key Points

  • Displacement is the shortest distance in a stated direction; distance is the full path length.
  • Slope of a distance-time graph = speed; slope of a speed-time graph = acceleration; area under a speed-time graph = distance.
  • Equations of motion: vf = vi + at; S = vi t + 1/2 at2; 2aS = vf2 - vi2.
  • Free fall: g = 9.8 m s-2 for every body, heavy or light.

lessons.title: Mass and Inertia
lessons.notes_html:
Dynamics is the part of mechanics that deals with the study of motion with reference to mass and force.

Mass

Mass is the quantity of matter in an object. It is a scalar quantity, measured in kilograms with a physical balance (beam balance), which compares the unknown mass with standard masses. Mass does not change from place to place.

Inertia

Inertia is the property of matter by which a body resists any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line. Mass is the measure of inertia: the greater the mass, the harder it is to change the object's state of motion.

Examples of Inertia

  • When a bus suddenly starts, passengers fall backwards, because their bodies tend to stay at rest.
  • When a moving bus suddenly stops, passengers fall forwards, because their bodies tend to keep moving. A man jumping from a moving bus falls in the direction of motion for the same reason.
  • Dust is removed from a carpet by beating it: the dust tends to stay at rest while the carpet moves.

lessons.title: Force and Types of Forces
lessons.notes_html:
Force is an agency that changes, or tends to change, the state of rest or of uniform motion of a body, or its shape. A force can start or stop motion, change speed or direction, or change shape or size. It is a vector quantity, measured in newtons (N).

Contact Forces

Contact forces act only when the bodies are in physical contact.

  • Friction between a book and a table.
  • The normal reaction of a table on a book resting on it.
  • Tension in a rope pulling a load.
  • Muscular force applied when pushing a cart.

Non-Contact Forces

Non-contact forces act without contact, through a field.

  • The gravitational force of the Earth pulling objects downwards.
  • The magnetic force between two magnets.
  • The electrostatic force between charged bodies.

lessons.title: Weight and Mass
lessons.notes_html:
Weight is the force with which the Earth (or another planet) attracts a body towards its centre. It is measured with a spring balance.

W = m × g

  • W — weight of the body (N)
  • m — mass of the body (kg)
  • g — acceleration due to gravity (9.8 m s-2 on Earth)
MassWeight
Quantity of matter in a bodyGravitational force on the body
Scalar quantityVector quantity
Measured in kilograms (kg)Measured in newtons (N)
Constant everywhereChanges with g: less on the Moon, zero in free space

Worked Example: Weight on Earth

The mass of an object is 1500 kg. What is its weight on Earth? Take g = 9.8 m s-2.

Step 1: W = m × g

Step 2: W = 1500 × 9.8 = 14700 N = 1.47 × 104 N.

Answer: 1.47 × 104 N

lessons.title: Gravity and the Fundamental Forces
lessons.notes_html:
Gravitational Field

The gravitational field is the region around a mass in which another mass experiences a gravitational force. Its strength at a point is the force per unit mass there:

  • Its SI unit is newton per kilogram (N kg-1), the same as m s-2.

Fundamental Forces of Nature

  • Gravitational force — the attraction between masses.
  • Electromagnetic force — the force between electric charges and magnets.
  • Strong nuclear force — holds protons and neutrons together in the nucleus.
  • Weak nuclear force — responsible for radioactive decay.

lessons.title: Newton's First and Second Laws of Motion
lessons.notes_html:
Newton's First Law (Law of Inertia)

A body remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an unbalanced external force. It is called the law of inertia: the body's inertia keeps it in its state until a net force changes it. For example, a book stays at rest on a table until someone pushes it, and a hockey puck slides on smooth ice at nearly constant velocity until friction or a stick stops it.

Newton's Second Law

When a net force acts on a body, the acceleration produced is directly proportional to the force and inversely proportional to the mass, and it takes place in the direction of the force.

F = m × a

  • F — net force (N)
  • m — mass (kg)
  • a — acceleration (m s-2)
  • A larger force gives a larger acceleration; a larger mass gives a smaller acceleration for the same force.
  • If the mass is doubled while the force stays constant, the acceleration becomes one half.

One Newton

One newton is the force which, acting on a mass of 1 kg, produces an acceleration of 1 m s-2 in the direction of the force: 1 N = 1 kg m s-2.

Worked Example: Acceleration of a Block

A block of 100 kg is pushed horizontally by a force of 250 N. Calculate the acceleration produced in the block.

Step 1: a = F / m

Step 2: a = 250 / 100 = 2.5 m s-2.

Answer: 2.5 m s-2

Worked Example: Braking of a Car

A car of mass 1500 kg is moving with a velocity of 20 m s-1. It is stopped in 5 seconds by applying brakes. Find (a) the average acceleration, (b) the force applied, (c) the distance covered.

Step 1: Average acceleration a = (0 - 20) / 5 = -4 m s-2 (magnitude 4 m s-2).

Step 2: Force F = m × a = 1500 × 4 = 6000 N.

Step 3: Distance S = average velocity × time = ((20 + 0) / 2) × 5 = 10 × 5 = 50 m.

Answer: (a) 4 m s-2, (b) 6000 N, (c) 50 m

lessons.title: Newton's Third Law and Its Limitations
lessons.notes_html:
Newton's Third Law

To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. When one body exerts a force (action) on a second body, the second body exerts an equal force (reaction) back on the first, in the opposite direction. The two forces act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other.

Examples

  • A rocket moves forward because it pushes exhaust gases backwards and the gases push the rocket forwards — the motion of a rocket is governed by the third law.
  • When you walk, your foot pushes the ground backwards and the ground pushes you forwards.
  • A gun recoils backwards when a bullet is fired forwards.

Limitations of Newton's Laws

Newton's laws describe everyday motion very well, but they need correction at speeds close to the speed of light (relativistic mechanics) and inside atoms (quantum mechanics).

mcqs.q: Newton's third law states: to every action there is:
options: A smaller reaction in the same direction
A reaction only on the same body
mcqs.why: Newton's third law: to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction, the second body exerting an equal force back in the opposite direction.

mcqs.q: Action and reaction forces never cancel each other because they:
options: Act only for a short time
mcqs.why: The two forces act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other, even though they are equal in size and opposite in direction.

mcqs.q: A rocket moves forward because:
options: It pushes exhaust gases backwards and the gases push the rocket forwards
Air pushes it from behind only
mcqs.why: The rocket pushes exhaust gases backwards and the gases push the rocket forwards, so rocket motion is governed by the third law.

mcqs.q: When you walk, you move forward because:
options: Your foot pushes the ground backwards and the ground pushes you forwards
The ground pulls you with gravity
Your mass pushes the air forwards
mcqs.why: When you walk, your foot pushes the ground backwards and the ground pushes you forwards, an action-reaction pair of the third law.

mcqs.q: A gun recoils backwards when a bullet is fired forwards. This is an example of:
mcqs.why: The gun exerts a forward force on the bullet and the bullet exerts an equal backward force on the gun, causing recoil, by the third law.

mcqs.q: Newton's laws need correction at speeds close to the speed of light. This is the field of:
mcqs.why: The limitations state Newton's laws need correction at speeds close to the speed of light, which is relativistic mechanics.

mcqs.q: Inside atoms, Newton's laws need correction by:
mcqs.why: The notes state Newton's laws need correction inside atoms, where quantum mechanics applies, as well as near light speed.

mcqs.q: Action and reaction are:
options: Equal in magnitude and in the same direction
Equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
Equal and acting on the same body
mcqs.why: Action and reaction are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, but they act on different bodies, as the third law states.

Rocket pushing gases back, gases pushing rocket forward

A puck sliding at constant velocity

mcqs.why: The limitations section states Newton's laws describe everyday motion very well, needing correction only near light speed and inside atoms.

lessons.title: States of Equilibrium
lessons.notes_html:
• Stable equilibrium — the body returns to its original position after a small displacement, e.g. a cone resting on its base.
  • Unstable equilibrium — a small displacement moves the body further away and it does not return, e.g. a cone balanced on its tip.
  • Neutral equilibrium — the body stays in its new position after displacement, e.g. a cone lying on its side, rolled slightly.

options: Moves further away and does not return
mcqs.why: In stable equilibrium the body returns to its original position after a small displacement, like a cone resting on its base.

mcqs.q: A cone resting on its base is in:
mcqs.why: The notes give a cone resting on its base as the example of stable equilibrium, returning to its position after a small displacement.

mcqs.q: A cone balanced on its tip is in:
mcqs.why: A cone balanced on its tip is in unstable equilibrium: a small displacement moves it further away and it does not return.

Leaves the body in the new position

mcqs.why: In neutral equilibrium the body stays in its new position after displacement, like a cone lying on its side rolled slightly.

mcqs.q: A cone lying on its side, rolled slightly, shows:
mcqs.why: The notes give a cone lying on its side as neutral equilibrium, because it stays in its new position after being rolled slightly.

mcqs.why: A cone resting on its base returns to its original position after a small displacement, which is stable equilibrium.

mcqs.why: A cone balanced on its tip does not return after a small displacement and moves further away, which is unstable equilibrium.

mcqs.why: Three states are described: stable, unstable and neutral equilibrium, each illustrated with a cone in a different position.

lessons.title: Friction: Static, Sliding and Rolling
lessons.notes_html:
Friction is the force that resists the relative motion (or the tendency to move) of one surface over another surface in contact with it. It acts parallel to the surfaces and opposite to the direction of motion, and it arises from the roughness and interlocking of the surfaces.

Static and Limiting Friction

  • Static friction — acts between two surfaces at rest relative to each other; it adjusts itself to balance the applied force, up to a maximum value.
  • Limiting friction — that maximum value of static friction, just before the surfaces start to slide.

Sliding (Kinetic) Friction

Sliding friction acts between two surfaces while they are sliding over each other. It is slightly less than limiting friction, it opposes the sliding motion, and its value is nearly independent of the sliding speed and of the area of contact.

Rolling Friction

Rolling friction acts when a body rolls over a surface, for example a wheel on a road. It is much less than sliding friction — the smallest of all — which is why wheels, ball bearings and rollers are used in machines and vehicles.

mcqs.q: Friction is the force that:
options: Resists the relative motion of one surface over another in contact with it
mcqs.why: Friction resists the relative motion, or tendency to move, of one surface over another in contact with it, acting parallel and opposite to motion.

mcqs.q: Friction acts:
options: Perpendicular to the surfaces, in the direction of motion
Parallel to the surfaces and opposite to the direction of motion
In the direction of motion only
mcqs.why: Friction acts parallel to the surfaces and opposite to the direction of motion, arising from roughness and interlocking of the surfaces.

mcqs.q: Static friction acts between two surfaces that are:
options: At rest relative to each other
mcqs.why: Static friction acts between two surfaces at rest relative to each other and adjusts itself to balance the applied force up to a maximum.

mcqs.q: Limiting friction is:
options: The smallest value of static friction
The maximum value of static friction, just before sliding starts
mcqs.why: Limiting friction is the maximum value of static friction, reached just before the surfaces start to slide over each other.

mcqs.q: Sliding (kinetic) friction is, compared to limiting friction:
mcqs.why: Sliding friction acts while surfaces slide and is slightly less than limiting friction, as stated in the notes for this lesson.

mcqs.q: Sliding friction is nearly independent of:
options: The sliding speed and the area of contact
mcqs.why: The value of sliding friction is nearly independent of the sliding speed and of the area of contact, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Rolling friction acts when a body:
options: Rolls over a surface, like a wheel on a road
Is at rest on a surface
mcqs.why: Rolling friction acts when a body rolls over a surface, for example a wheel on a road, and it is much less than sliding friction.

mcqs.q: Which friction is the smallest of all?
mcqs.why: Rolling friction is much less than sliding friction, the smallest of all, which is why wheels, ball bearings and rollers are used.

mcqs.q: Friction arises from:
options: The roughness and interlocking of the surfaces
mcqs.why: Friction arises from the roughness and interlocking of the surfaces in contact, as stated in the definition in the notes.

mcqs.q: Wheels and ball bearings are used in machines because they replace sliding with rolling, which:
mcqs.why: Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction, so wheels, ball bearings and rollers greatly reduce friction in machines and vehicles.

lessons.title: Advantages, Disadvantages and Reducing Friction
lessons.notes_html:
Advantages of Friction

  • We can walk and run without slipping.
  • Vehicles can move and brake on roads.
  • We can grip and hold objects, and write with a pen.
  • Nails and screws stay fixed in wood.
  • Belts drive machines without slipping.

Disadvantages of Friction

  • It wastes energy as heat and reduces the efficiency of machines.
  • It wears out moving parts such as tyres, brake pads and engine parts.
  • It opposes motion, so extra force and fuel are needed.
  • It produces unwanted noise and heat.

Methods of Reducing Friction

  • Use lubricants such as oil or grease between moving parts.
  • Use ball bearings or rollers to replace sliding with rolling.
  • Polish and smooth the surfaces in contact.
  • Streamline the shape of fast-moving bodies.
  • Use an air cushion where possible.

Key Points

  • Mass is constant everywhere; weight = mg and changes with g.
  • Newton's laws: (1) inertia, (2) F = ma, (3) action and reaction are equal and opposite.
  • Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction.
  • Lubricants and ball bearings are used to reduce friction.

mcqs.q: Which is an advantage of friction?
options: We can walk and run without slipping
It wears out tyres and brake pads
mcqs.why: An advantage of friction is that we can walk and run without slipping; vehicles can also move and brake on roads because of friction.

mcqs.q: Nails and screws stay fixed in wood because of:
mcqs.why: The notes list as an advantage of friction that nails and screws stay fixed in wood, and we can grip objects and write with a pen.

options: It wastes energy as heat and reduces efficiency
We can grip and hold objects
mcqs.why: A disadvantage is that friction wastes energy as heat and reduces the efficiency of machines, and it wears out moving parts.

mcqs.q: Friction wears out moving parts such as:
options: Tyres, brake pads and engine parts
mcqs.why: The disadvantages list states friction wears out moving parts such as tyres, brake pads and engine parts, and needs extra force and fuel.

mcqs.q: Belts drive machines without slipping because of:
options: The weight of the belt alone
mcqs.why: Belts drive machines without slipping is listed as an advantage of friction between the belt and the machine parts it drives.

mcqs.q: Which method reduces friction by replacing sliding with rolling?
options: Using lubricants like oil or grease
mcqs.why: Ball bearings or rollers replace sliding with rolling, and rolling friction is much smaller, so friction is greatly reduced.

mcqs.q: Oil or grease used between moving parts are called:
mcqs.why: Lubricants such as oil or grease between moving parts are a method of reducing friction listed in the notes for this lesson.

mcqs.q: Streamlining the shape of fast-moving bodies is a method to:
mcqs.why: Streamline the shape of fast-moving bodies is listed among the methods of reducing friction, along with lubricants and polishing.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a method of reducing friction listed in the notes?
mcqs.why: Reducing methods are lubricants, ball bearings, polishing and smoothing, streamlining and air cushions; making surfaces rougher would increase friction.

mcqs.q: Friction opposes motion, so because of it:
options: Less force and fuel are needed
Extra force and fuel are needed
mcqs.why: A disadvantage listed is that friction opposes motion, so extra force and fuel are needed, and it produces unwanted noise and heat.

lessons.title: Momentum
lessons.notes_html:
Momentum is the quantity of motion in an object, defined as the product of its mass and its velocity.

p = m × v

  • p — momentum (kg m s-1)
  • m — mass (kg)
  • v — velocity (m s-1)
  • Momentum is a vector quantity: its direction is always along the velocity.
  • Its SI unit is kilogram metre per second (kg m s-1), the same as newton second (N s).

A cricket ball and a tennis ball moving with the same velocity do not have the same momentum: the cricket ball has a much larger mass, so its momentum is much larger, and a much larger impulse is needed to stop it.

Worked Example: Momentum of a Sprinter

The mass of a sprinter is 45 kg. What will be his momentum if he runs at a velocity of 36 km h-1?

Step 1: Convert velocity: 36 km h-1 = 36 / 3.6 = 10 m s-1.

Step 2: p = m × v = 45 × 10 = 450 kg m s-1.

Answer: 450 kg m s-1

mcqs.q: What is momentum defined as?
mcqs.why: Momentum is the quantity of motion, defined as p = m x v, the product of mass and velocity.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for momentum?
mcqs.why: The notes give p = m x v, where m is mass in kg and v is velocity in m/s.

mcqs.q: What is the SI unit of momentum?
mcqs.why: Momentum p = m x v has unit kg x m/s = kg m/s, which is the same as the newton second, N s.

mcqs.q: Momentum is which type of quantity?
mcqs.why: Momentum is a vector quantity and its direction is always along the direction of the velocity.

mcqs.q: A sprinter of mass 45 kg runs at 36 km/h. What is his momentum?
mcqs.why: Convert velocity: 36 / 3.6 = 10 m/s. Then p = m x v = 45 x 10 = 450 kg m/s.

mcqs.q: Convert 36 km/h to m/s as used in the sprinter example.
mcqs.why: To convert km/h to m/s divide by 3.6: velocity = 36 / 3.6 = 10 m/s.

mcqs.q: A cricket ball and a tennis ball move with the same velocity. Which has larger momentum?
options: The cricket ball, because it has much larger mass
The tennis ball, because it is lighter
mcqs.why: At the same velocity, p = m x v is larger for larger mass, so the heavier cricket ball has much larger momentum.

mcqs.q: Why is a larger impulse needed to stop a cricket ball than a tennis ball at the same velocity?
options: Because the cricket ball has no momentum
Because the cricket ball has much larger momentum
Because the tennis ball moves faster
Because momentum does not depend on mass
mcqs.why: The cricket ball has much larger mass and therefore much larger momentum, so a much larger impulse is needed to stop it.

mcqs.q: If a body of mass 45 kg moves at 10 m/s, what is p = m x v?
mcqs.why: p = m x v = 45 x 10 = 450 kg m/s, the same calculation as the sprinter worked example.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the direction of momentum is correct?
options: It is opposite to the velocity
It is perpendicular to the velocity
It has no direction at all
It is always along the velocity
mcqs.why: Momentum is a vector quantity whose direction is always along the velocity of the moving object.

lessons.title: Law of Conservation of Momentum
lessons.notes_html:
An isolated system is a system on which no external (outside) force acts, so its total momentum stays constant. Examples: two colliding billiard balls on a smooth table (ignoring friction), or a bullet and gun taken together before and after firing.

The Law

The total momentum of an isolated system remains the same (constant), provided no external force acts upon it. In a collision, the total momentum before the collision equals the total momentum after the collision.

Recoil of a Gun

Before firing, the total momentum of the gun and bullet is zero. When the bullet goes forward with momentum mv, the gun must gain an equal momentum in the opposite direction so that the total stays zero. That backward motion of the gun is its recoil.

Worked Example: Recoil Speed of a Rifle

A rifle has a mass of 5.0 kg. It fires a bullet of 8 g with a speed of 400 m s-1. Calculate the recoil speed of the gun.

Step 1: Bullet mass = 8 g = 0.008 kg; bullet momentum = 0.008 × 400 = 3.2 kg m s-1.

Step 2: By conservation of momentum, the gun's momentum = -3.2 kg m s-1.

Step 3: Recoil speed = 3.2 / 5.0 = 0.64 m s-1 in the opposite direction.

Answer: 0.64 m s-1 backwards

mcqs.q: What is an isolated system?
options: A system with a large external force on it
A system on which no external force acts
A system containing only one body
A system that is always at rest
mcqs.why: An isolated system is a system on which no external outside force acts, so its total momentum stays constant.

mcqs.q: What does the law of conservation of momentum state?
options: Total momentum increases in a collision
Total momentum becomes zero after a collision
Total momentum of an isolated system remains constant if no external force acts
Momentum of each body always stays the same
mcqs.why: The total momentum of an isolated system remains the same provided no external force acts upon it.

mcqs.q: In a collision in an isolated system, how do total momenta before and after compare?
mcqs.why: In a collision, the total momentum before the collision equals the total momentum after the collision.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of an isolated system given in the notes?
options: Two colliding billiard balls on a smooth table, ignoring friction
A car braking on a rough road
A ball falling under gravity alone
A book pushed across a table
mcqs.why: Two colliding billiard balls on a smooth table, ignoring friction, are given as an example of an isolated system.

mcqs.q: What is the total momentum of a gun and bullet before firing?
options: Equal to the bullet momentum after firing
Equal to the gun momentum after firing
mcqs.why: Before firing both gun and bullet are at rest, so the total momentum of gun and bullet is zero.

mcqs.q: What is recoil of a gun?
options: The forward motion of the bullet only
The heating of the gun barrel
The backward motion of the gun after firing
mcqs.why: When the bullet goes forward, the gun gains equal momentum backwards so total stays zero; that backward motion is recoil.

mcqs.q: A rifle of mass 5.0 kg fires a bullet of 8 g at 400 m/s. What is the bullet momentum?
mcqs.why: Bullet mass = 8 g = 0.008 kg. Bullet momentum = 0.008 x 400 = 3.2 kg m/s.

mcqs.q: For the rifle example, what is the recoil speed of the gun?
mcqs.why: Gun momentum must be 3.2 kg m/s backwards. Recoil speed = 3.2 / 5.0 = 0.64 m/s in the opposite direction.

mcqs.q: In the rifle example, the gun momentum after firing is:
options: -3.2 kg m/s, opposite to the bullet
mcqs.why: By conservation of momentum the gun momentum = -3.2 kg m/s, equal in size and opposite in direction to the bullet.

mcqs.q: When does total momentum stay constant?
options: Only when bodies are at rest
Only when a large external force acts
Provided no external force acts on the system
mcqs.why: Total momentum remains constant provided no external force acts upon the isolated system.

lessons.title: Momentum and Newton's Second Law
lessons.notes_html:
In terms of momentum, Newton's second law states: the force acting on a body is equal to the rate of change of its momentum, and the change takes place in the direction of the applied force.

F = change in momentum / time

Worked Example: Force from Change of Momentum

An object of mass 50 kg is moving with a velocity of 10 m s-1. A constant force increases its velocity to 20 m s-1 in 5 seconds. Calculate the magnitude of the applied force.

Step 1: Change in momentum = 50 × (20 - 10) = 500 kg m s-1.

Step 2: F = change in momentum / time = 500 / 5 = 100 N.

Answer: 100 N

mcqs.q: How does Newton's second law state force in terms of momentum?
options: Force equals rate of change of momentum
Force equals momentum divided by mass
Force equals momentum multiplied by time
Force equals change in velocity only
mcqs.why: In terms of momentum, force is equal to the rate of change of momentum, in the direction of the applied force.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for force from momentum change?
options: F = change in momentum x time
mcqs.why: The notes give F = change in momentum / time, the rate at which momentum changes.

mcqs.q: In which direction does the momentum change take place?
options: In the direction of the applied force
mcqs.why: The change in momentum takes place in the direction of the applied force, as stated in the momentum form of the second law.

mcqs.q: An object of mass 50 kg increases velocity from 10 m/s to 20 m/s. What is the change in momentum?
mcqs.why: Change in momentum = m x (change in velocity) = 50 x (20 - 10) = 50 x 10 = 500 kg m/s.

mcqs.q: The same object changes momentum by 500 kg m/s in 5 seconds. What is the force?
mcqs.why: F = change in momentum / time = 500 / 5 = 100 N, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: A constant force increases the velocity of a 50 kg object from 10 m/s to 20 m/s in 5 s. The force is:
mcqs.why: Change in momentum = 50 x (20 - 10) = 500 kg m/s. Then F = 500 / 5 = 100 N.

mcqs.q: If the same momentum change happens in a longer time, what happens to the force?
mcqs.why: Since F = change in momentum / time, a larger time for the same momentum change gives a smaller force.

mcqs.q: What are the quantities in the worked example for force from momentum change?
options: Mass 5 kg, time 100 s, force 5 N
Mass 100 kg, time 10 s, force 500 N
Mass 20 kg, time 2 s, force 50 N
Mass 50 kg, time 5 s, force 100 N
mcqs.why: The worked example uses mass 50 kg, velocity change 10 to 20 m/s in 5 seconds, giving a force of 100 N.

mcqs.q: Rate of change of momentum means:
options: Change in momentum divided by time taken
Change in velocity divided by mass
mcqs.why: Rate means per unit time, so rate of change of momentum = change in momentum / time, which equals the force.

mcqs.q: According to the momentum form of the second law, a larger rate of change of momentum means:
mcqs.why: Force equals the rate of change of momentum, so a larger rate of change of momentum corresponds to a larger force.

lessons.title: Impulse of a Force
lessons.notes_html:
When a large force F acts on an object for an extremely short interval of time, the product of the force and the time is called the impulse of the force.

Impulse = F × Δt

  • Impulse equals the change in momentum produced: impulse = m × (change in velocity).
  • Its SI unit is the newton second (N s), the same as kg m s-1.
  • A moving object has momentum, not impulse: impulse is produced only while a force acts.

Impulse in Daily Life

  • A cricket player lowers his hands while catching a fast ball: the time of the catch increases, so the force on his hands is smaller.
  • Heavy vehicles have spring suspension, which increases the time of a jerk and reduces the force.
  • A karate player breaks a brick with a very short, hard blow: a large force acts for a very short time.

Worked Example: Impact Time

An object of mass 250 g is moving at a velocity of 64.8 km h-1. What is its initial momentum? Calculate the impact time if a force of 9 kN is needed to stop the object.

Step 1: Convert: mass = 0.25 kg; velocity = 64.8 / 3.6 = 18 m s-1.

Step 2: Initial momentum = 0.25 × 18 = 4.5 kg m s-1.

Step 3: Impulse to stop = 4.5 = F × Δt, so Δt = 4.5 / 9000 = 5.0 × 10-4 s.

Answer: momentum 4.5 kg m s-1; impact time 5.0 × 10-4 s

Key Points

  • Momentum p = mv; it is a vector along the velocity.
  • In an isolated system the total momentum never changes.
  • Force = rate of change of momentum.
  • Impulse = F × Δt = change in momentum.

mcqs.q: What is the impulse of a force?
options: Product of force and the short time it acts
Change in velocity divided by time
mcqs.why: When a large force acts for a very short time, impulse = F x delta t, the product of force and time.

mcqs.q: Impulse equals which quantity?
mcqs.why: Impulse equals the change in momentum produced, and also impulse = m x (change in velocity).

mcqs.q: What is the SI unit of impulse?
options: kg m/s only, with no other form
mcqs.why: The SI unit of impulse is the newton second, N s, which is the same as kg m/s, the unit of momentum change.

mcqs.q: A moving object has which of these, not impulse?
options: A change in momentum at rest
mcqs.why: A moving object has momentum, not impulse; impulse is produced only while a force acts on the object.

mcqs.q: Why does a cricket player lower his hands while catching a fast ball?
options: To decrease the time of the catch
To increase the time of the catch so the force on his hands is smaller
To increase the force on his hands
To increase the momentum of the ball
mcqs.why: Lowering the hands increases the time of the catch, so for the same momentum change the force on his hands is smaller.

mcqs.q: How does spring suspension in heavy vehicles help?
options: It decreases the time of a jerk
It increases the force of a jerk
It increases the time of a jerk and reduces the force
It removes the momentum of the vehicle
mcqs.why: Spring suspension increases the time of a jerk, which reduces the force for the same change in momentum.

mcqs.q: How does a karate player break a brick?
options: With a small force over a long time
With a slow push over a long time
With a very short, hard blow: a large force for a very short time
mcqs.why: A karate player uses a very short, hard blow, so a large force acts for a very short time to break the brick.

mcqs.q: An object of mass 250 g moves at 64.8 km/h. What is its initial momentum?
mcqs.why: Mass = 0.25 kg and velocity = 64.8 / 3.6 = 18 m/s. Initial momentum = 0.25 x 18 = 4.5 kg m/s.

mcqs.q: Convert 64.8 km/h to m/s for the impact-time example.
mcqs.why: To convert km/h to m/s divide by 3.6: velocity = 64.8 / 3.6 = 18 m/s.

mcqs.q: If a force of 9 kN is needed to stop an object with momentum 4.5 kg m/s, what is the impact time?
mcqs.why: Impulse to stop = 4.5 = F x delta t, so delta t = 4.5 / 9000 = 0.0005 s, which is 5.0 x 10^-4 s.

lessons.title: Like and Unlike Parallel Forces
lessons.notes_html:
Parallel forces are forces whose lines of action are parallel to each other, whether they act in the same direction or in opposite directions.

  • Like parallel forces — parallel forces acting in the same direction; their resultant is the sum of the forces.
  • Unlike parallel forces — parallel forces acting in opposite directions; their resultant is the difference of the forces, acting in the direction of the larger force.

For example, the two forces of a couple acting on a steering wheel are parallel forces.

mcqs.q: What are parallel forces?
options: Forces whose lines of action are parallel to each other
Forces that always act at a point
Forces that are always equal in size
Forces that act only at right angles
mcqs.why: Parallel forces are forces whose lines of action are parallel to each other, in the same or opposite directions.

mcqs.q: What are like parallel forces?
options: Parallel forces acting in opposite directions
Parallel forces acting in the same direction
Forces acting along the same line only
mcqs.why: Like parallel forces are parallel forces acting in the same direction, and their resultant is the sum of the forces.

mcqs.q: What is the resultant of like parallel forces?
mcqs.why: For like parallel forces acting in the same direction, the resultant is the sum of the forces.

mcqs.q: What are unlike parallel forces?
options: Forces acting in the same direction
Forces whose resultant is their sum
Parallel forces acting in opposite directions
mcqs.why: Unlike parallel forces are parallel forces acting in opposite directions, so their resultant is the difference.

mcqs.q: What is the resultant of unlike parallel forces?
options: The difference of the forces, in the direction of the larger force
mcqs.why: For unlike parallel forces the resultant is the difference of the forces, acting in the direction of the larger force.

mcqs.q: Two like parallel forces of 20 N and 10 N act in the same direction. What is their resultant?
mcqs.why: Resultant of like parallel forces = sum = 20 + 10 = 30 N, using the sum rule given in the notes.

mcqs.q: Two unlike parallel forces of 20 N and 10 N act in opposite directions. What is their resultant?
options: 10 N in the direction of the larger force
mcqs.why: Resultant of unlike parallel forces = difference = 20 - 10 = 10 N, in the direction of the larger force.

mcqs.q: The two forces of a couple acting on a steering wheel are an example of:
mcqs.why: The notes give the two forces of a couple acting on a steering wheel as an example of parallel forces.

mcqs.q: If unlike parallel forces are exactly equal, what is their resultant difference?
options: 0, because difference = larger minus smaller with equal sizes
mcqs.why: Resultant = difference of the forces. For equal unlike forces, difference = F - F = 0.

mcqs.q: In which direction does the resultant of unlike parallel forces act?
options: In the direction of the larger force
In the direction of the smaller force
mcqs.why: The resultant of unlike parallel forces is their difference and acts in the direction of the larger force.

lessons.title: Moment of Force or Torque
lessons.notes_html:
The moment of force, or torque, is the turning effect of a force about a point or axis.

Torque = F × d

  • F — applied force (N)
  • d — moment arm: the perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force (m)
  • The SI unit of torque is the newton metre (N m).
  • By convention, an anticlockwise torque is taken as positive and a clockwise torque as negative.

Torque in Daily Life

  • Opening a door by pushing its handle, far from the hinges.
  • Loosening a nut with a spanner.
  • Turning a steering wheel.
  • A see-saw balanced on its pivot.

A long spanner is preferred for a tight nut: with a larger moment arm, the same force produces a larger torque, so the nut can be loosened with less effort.

Worked Example: Torque on a Spanner

A force of 150 N is applied perpendicularly on a spanner at a distance of 20 cm from the nut. Calculate the torque produced.

Step 1: Convert distance: 20 cm = 0.20 m.

Step 2: Torque = F × d = 150 × 0.20 = 30 N m.

Answer: 30 N m

mcqs.q: What is torque, or moment of force?
options: The pushing effect of a force in a straight line
The turning effect of a force about a point or axis
The weight of a body about its centre
The speed of rotation of a body
mcqs.why: The moment of force, or torque, is the turning effect of a force about a point or axis.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for torque?
mcqs.why: The notes give Torque = F x d, where F is the applied force and d is the moment arm.

mcqs.q: What is the moment arm, d?
options: The length of the spanner handle only
The distance along the force direction
The perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force
mcqs.why: The moment arm is the perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force, in metres.

mcqs.q: What is the SI unit of torque?
mcqs.why: Torque = F x d has unit N x m = N m, the newton metre, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: By convention, which torque is taken as positive?
mcqs.why: By convention an anticlockwise torque is taken as positive and a clockwise torque as negative.

mcqs.q: By convention, a clockwise torque is taken as:
mcqs.why: The notes state that an anticlockwise torque is positive and a clockwise torque is taken as negative.

mcqs.q: A force of 150 N is applied perpendicularly at 20 cm from a nut. What is the torque?
mcqs.why: Distance = 20 cm = 0.20 m. Torque = F x d = 150 x 0.20 = 30 N m.

mcqs.q: Why is a long spanner preferred for a tight nut?
options: With a larger moment arm, the same force produces a larger torque
A long spanner increases the force applied
A long spanner reduces the moment arm
A long spanner changes the unit of torque
mcqs.why: With a larger moment arm d, Torque = F x d is larger for the same force, so the nut loosens with less effort.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of torque in daily life from the notes?
options: A book resting on a table
Opening a door by pushing its handle, far from the hinges
A car moving in a straight line
mcqs.why: Opening a door by pushing its handle far from the hinges is listed as a daily-life example of torque.

mcqs.q: If the moment arm is larger, for the same force the torque is:
mcqs.why: Torque = F x d, so increasing d with the same F increases the torque, which is why a long spanner works better.

lessons.title: Principle of Moments
lessons.notes_html:
The principle of moments states: a body is at rest (in rotational equilibrium) if the sum of all clockwise torques about any point is equal to the sum of all anticlockwise torques about that point.

Worked Example: A Balanced Rod

A uniform rod AB is balanced at point C. A force of 20 N is applied at point A. Find the force F to be applied at B to balance the rod. (AC = 10 m, CB = 5 m; both forces act downwards.)

Step 1: By the principle of moments about C, clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment.

Step 2: 20 × 10 = F × 5.

Step 3: F = 200 / 5 = 40 N.

Answer: 40 N

mcqs.q: What does the principle of moments state?
options: Clockwise torques are always greater than anticlockwise torques
A body in rotational equilibrium has sum of clockwise torques equal to sum of anticlockwise torques about any point
All torques about a point must be zero individually
Torque equals force divided by distance
mcqs.why: A body is in rotational equilibrium if the sum of clockwise torques about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise torques.

mcqs.q: A body is at rest in rotational equilibrium when:
options: Only clockwise torques act on it
Only anticlockwise torques act on it
Sum of clockwise torques equals sum of anticlockwise torques about a point
No forces act on it at all
mcqs.why: The principle of moments requires clockwise moments = anticlockwise moments about the pivot for balance.

mcqs.q: A uniform rod AB is balanced at C, with a 20 N force at A where AC = 10 m. What is the clockwise or anticlockwise moment of the 20 N force about C?
mcqs.why: Moment about C = force x distance = 20 x 10 = 200 N m, which must be balanced by the moment of F at B.

mcqs.q: For the balanced rod, CB = 5 m. What force F at B balances the 20 N at A?
mcqs.why: By principle of moments: 20 x 10 = F x 5, so F = 200 / 5 = 40 N.

mcqs.q: In the balanced rod example, both forces act in which direction?
options: One up and one down horizontally
mcqs.why: The worked example states that both the 20 N force at A and the force F at B act downwards on the rod.

mcqs.q: About which point are moments taken in the balanced rod example?
options: Point C, the pivot where the rod is balanced
The midpoint of AB only as a force
mcqs.why: Moments are taken about C, the pivot point at which the uniform rod AB is balanced.

mcqs.q: Which equation expresses the principle of moments for the rod example?
mcqs.why: Clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment about C gives 20 x 10 = F x 5, leading to F = 40 N.

mcqs.q: If 20 x 10 = F x 5, what is the step to find F?
mcqs.why: 20 x 10 = 200, and F = 200 / 5 = 40 N, as shown in the worked example steps.

mcqs.q: What does rotational equilibrium mean in this lesson?
options: The body spins faster and faster
The body is at rest because clockwise and anticlockwise torques balance
The body moves in a straight line
mcqs.why: In rotational equilibrium the body is at rest because the sum of clockwise torques equals the sum of anticlockwise torques.

mcqs.q: To balance a larger moment on one side of a pivot with a smaller distance on the other side, the force needed is:
options: Larger, because force x distance must match the other moment
mcqs.why: In the example, F acts at only 5 m versus 10 m, so F must be larger: F = 200 / 5 = 40 N versus 20 N.

lessons.title: Centre of Gravity
lessons.notes_html:
The centre of gravity of a body is the point at which the whole weight of the body appears to act vertically downwards towards the centre of the Earth.

Centre of Gravity of Regular Objects

  • A uniform rod: at its midpoint.
  • A uniform disc: at its centre.

Centre of Gravity of an Irregular Plane Lamina

Hang the lamina freely from a pin through a hole near one edge and draw the vertical line from the pin with the help of a plumb line. Repeat from two other holes. The three lines cross at one point: the centre of gravity.

mcqs.q: What is the centre of gravity of a body?
options: The point where half the weight acts upwards
The point at which the whole weight appears to act vertically downwards towards the centre of the Earth
The geometric centre in every case
The point where the body is hung from
mcqs.why: The centre of gravity is the point at which the whole weight of the body appears to act vertically downwards towards the centre of the Earth.

mcqs.q: Where is the centre of gravity of a uniform rod?
options: At one end of the rod
At a quarter of its length
mcqs.why: For a uniform rod, the centre of gravity is at its midpoint, as given for regular objects in the notes.

mcqs.q: Where is the centre of gravity of a uniform disc?
mcqs.why: For a uniform disc, the centre of gravity is at its centre, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: How is the centre of gravity of an irregular plane lamina found first?
options: Hang it freely from a pin through a hole near one edge and draw the vertical line from the pin using a plumb line
Weigh it on a balance and halve the weight
Measure its area and divide by two
Balance it on a fingertip only
mcqs.why: Hang the lamina freely from a pin through a hole near one edge and draw the vertical line from the pin with a plumb line.

mcqs.q: What is used to draw the vertical line in the lamina experiment?
mcqs.why: The vertical line from the pin is drawn with the help of a plumb line, which hangs vertically downwards.

mcqs.q: After the first hole, what is repeated in the lamina method?
options: The lamina is cut into pieces
The hanging and line drawing is repeated from two other holes
mcqs.why: The process is repeated from two other holes, giving three lines in total on the lamina.

mcqs.q: How is the centre of gravity located from the lines on the lamina?
options: It is at the end of the first line
It is midway along one line
It is outside all the lines
The three lines cross at one point, which is the centre of gravity
mcqs.why: The three vertical lines drawn from three holes cross at one point, and that crossing point is the centre of gravity.

mcqs.q: In which direction does the weight appear to act at the centre of gravity?
options: Vertically downwards towards the centre of the Earth
Vertically upwards away from the Earth
In a circle around the body
mcqs.why: At the centre of gravity the whole weight appears to act vertically downwards towards the centre of the Earth.

mcqs.q: How many holes are used in total in the lamina method described?
options: Three holes: one near an edge and two other holes
mcqs.why: The lamina is hung from a hole near one edge and then from two other holes, so three holes and three lines are used.

mcqs.q: The lamina in the centre of gravity method is described as:
mcqs.why: The plumb-line method is given for the centre of gravity of an irregular plane lamina, unlike the rod and disc.

lessons.title: Centre of Gravity and Stability; Rotating Objects
lessons.notes_html:
Position of Centre of Gravity and Stability

The lower the centre of gravity of an object, the more stable the object: it is harder to topple, because tilting it raises its centre of gravity only slightly and the vertical line through it stays inside its base. A high centre of gravity makes an object less stable: a small tilt moves that vertical line outside the base and the object topples over.

Improving Stability

  • Lower the centre of gravity, e.g. load heavy luggage at the bottom of a bus.
  • Increase the base area, e.g. a racing car is built wide and low.

Applications

  • Intercity buses carry luggage at the bottom, so the bus does not topple on turns.
  • Racing cars are built low and wide, so they can take curves at high speed without toppling.
  • Balancing toys are made so that their centre of gravity stays below the pivot point, so they always return upright.

Motion of Rotating Objects

A rotating object turns about a fixed point or axis, with all its particles moving in circles around that axis. Without a net external torque it keeps rotating at the same rate; a net torque in the direction of rotation speeds it up, and a net torque against it slows it down, until friction finally brings it to rest.

Key Points

  • Torque = force × moment arm; its unit is N m.
  • For balance: clockwise moments = anticlockwise moments about the pivot.
  • A low centre of gravity and a wide base make an object more stable.

mcqs.q: How does the position of the centre of gravity affect stability?
options: Higher centre of gravity means more stable
Centre of gravity has no effect on stability
Lower centre of gravity means more stable
mcqs.why: The lower the centre of gravity, the more stable the object, because it is harder to topple.

mcqs.q: Why is a low centre of gravity more stable?
options: Tilting lowers its centre of gravity a lot
Tilting moves the vertical line outside the base at once
Tilting raises its centre of gravity only slightly and the vertical line through it stays inside its base
mcqs.why: With a low centre of gravity, tilting raises it only slightly and the vertical line through it stays inside the base.

mcqs.q: What happens with a high centre of gravity on a small tilt?
options: A small tilt moves the vertical line outside the base and the object topples over
mcqs.why: A high centre of gravity makes an object less stable: a small tilt moves the vertical line outside the base and it topples.

mcqs.q: Which is a way to improve stability given in the notes?
options: Lower the centre of gravity, for example load heavy luggage at the bottom of a bus
Load heavy luggage on top of a bus
mcqs.why: Lowering the centre of gravity improves stability, for example by loading heavy luggage at the bottom of a bus.

mcqs.q: How does increasing the base area improve stability?
options: It raises the centre of gravity
It reduces the weight of the object
A wider base helps keep the vertical line through the centre of gravity inside the base, as with a wide racing car
It removes the need for a centre of gravity
mcqs.why: Increasing the base area improves stability; a racing car is built wide and low so it does not topple on curves.

mcqs.q: Why do intercity buses carry luggage at the bottom?
options: To raise the centre of gravity
To make the bus lighter on top only
To increase the base width of the road
So the bus does not topple on turns, by keeping the centre of gravity low
mcqs.why: Buses carry luggage at the bottom to lower the centre of gravity, so the bus does not topple on turns.

mcqs.q: Why are racing cars built low and wide?
options: So they can take curves at high speed without toppling
To raise their centre of gravity for speed
To make them topple more easily
mcqs.why: Racing cars are built low and wide to lower the centre of gravity and widen the base, so they take curves without toppling.

mcqs.q: Why do balancing toys always return upright?
options: Their centre of gravity is above the pivot
Their centre of gravity stays below the pivot point
They have no centre of gravity
They have a very narrow base
mcqs.why: Balancing toys are made so their centre of gravity stays below the pivot point, so they always return upright.

mcqs.q: What happens to a rotating object with no net external torque?
options: It keeps rotating at the same rate
It moves in a straight line
mcqs.why: Without a net external torque a rotating object keeps rotating at the same rate, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: What does a net torque against the rotation do?
options: It has no effect on rotation
It reverses the mass of the object
It slows the rotation down, until friction finally brings it to rest
mcqs.why: A net torque against rotation slows it down, and a torque in the direction of rotation speeds it up, until friction stops it.

lessons.title: Circular Motion and Centripetal Force
lessons.notes_html:
Circular motion is the motion of an object along a circular path. Its speed may stay constant, but its velocity keeps changing because its direction changes at every point, so it is accelerated motion even at constant speed.

Centripetal Force

Centripetal force is the force that keeps a body moving in a circle. It is always directed towards the centre of the circle, along the radius, and it is perpendicular to the velocity at every point — which is why it changes the direction of motion without changing the speed. Without it, the body would fly off along a tangent.

Fc = m v2 / r

  • Fc — centripetal force (N)
  • m — mass of the body (kg)
  • v — speed of the body along the circle (m s-1)
  • r — radius of the circle (m)
  • The centripetal acceleration is ac = v2 / r, also towards the centre.
  • More force is needed if the mass or the speed increases, or the radius decreases: Fc grows with the square of the speed.

Worked Example: Centripetal Force

A mass of 5 kg is kept moving in a circle of radius 2 m with a constant speed of 10 m s-1. Find the centripetal force.

Step 1: Fc = m v2 / r

Step 2: Fc = 5 × 102 / 2 = 5 × 100 / 2 = 250 N.

Answer: 250 N

mcqs.q: What is circular motion?
options: Motion of an object along a circular path
Motion in a straight line only
To-and-fro motion about a mean position
Motion with no change in direction
mcqs.why: Circular motion is the motion of an object along a circular path, as defined at the start of the lesson.

mcqs.q: In circular motion at constant speed, why is the motion accelerated?
options: Because the velocity keeps changing as direction changes at every point
mcqs.why: Speed may stay constant, but velocity keeps changing because direction changes at every point, so it is accelerated motion.

mcqs.q: What is centripetal force?
options: A force directed away from the centre
A force along the tangent only
The force that keeps a body moving in a circle
A force that increases the speed only
mcqs.why: Centripetal force is the force that keeps a body moving in a circle, directed towards the centre of the circle.

mcqs.q: In which direction does centripetal force act?
options: Towards the centre of the circle, along the radius
mcqs.why: Centripetal force is always directed towards the centre of the circle, along the radius, at every point.

mcqs.q: What is the relation of centripetal force to the velocity?
options: It is perpendicular to the velocity at every point
It is parallel to the velocity
It is opposite to the velocity
It acts at 45 degrees to the velocity
mcqs.why: Centripetal force is perpendicular to the velocity at every point, which is why it changes direction without changing speed.

mcqs.q: Without centripetal force, what would the body do?
mcqs.why: Without centripetal force the body would fly off along a tangent to the circular path.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for centripetal force?
mcqs.why: The notes give Fc = m v squared / r, where m is mass, v is speed and r is radius of the circle.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for centripetal acceleration?
options: ac = v squared / r, towards the centre
ac = v / r, away from the centre
mcqs.why: Centripetal acceleration is ac = v squared / r, and it is also directed towards the centre of the circle.

mcqs.q: A mass of 5 kg moves in a circle of radius 2 m at 10 m/s. What is the centripetal force?
mcqs.why: Fc = m v squared / r = 5 x 10 squared / 2 = 5 x 100 / 2 = 500 / 2 = 250 N.

options: Mass or speed increases, or radius decreases
mcqs.q: More centripetal force is needed when:
mcqs.why: From Fc = m v squared / r, force increases with mass, grows with the square of the speed, and increases when radius decreases.

lessons.title: Centrifugal Force and Real-Life Examples
lessons.notes_html:
Centrifugal Force

Centrifugal force is a fictitious (apparent) force that appears to act on a body moving in a circle. It is equal in magnitude to the centripetal force but directed away from the centre, along the radius, and it exists only as long as the body moves in the circle. Passengers in a bus taking a turn feel thrown outwards, away from the centre of the turn.

Real-Life Examples of Centripetal Force

  • The tension in the string keeps a whirled stone moving in its circular path.
  • Friction between tyres and road provides the centripetal force for a car taking a turn; banking of roads helps provide it safely.
  • The Earth's gravity provides the centripetal force keeping the Moon in its orbit.

Worked Example: Centripetal Acceleration of an Aeroplane

An aeroplane is moving in a circle of radius 25 km at constant height at a speed of 270 km h-1. Calculate the centripetal acceleration acting on the aeroplane.

Step 1: Convert: v = 270 / 3.6 = 75 m s-1; r = 25 km = 25,000 m.

Step 2: ac = v2 / r = 752 / 25,000 = 5625 / 25,000 = 0.225 m s-2.

Answer: 0.225 m s-2

Key Points

  • Centripetal force always acts towards the centre of the circle.
  • Fc = mv2 / r and ac = v2 / r.
  • Centrifugal force is the apparent force directed away from the centre.

mcqs.q: What is centrifugal force?
options: A real force towards the centre
A fictitious apparent force that appears to act on a body moving in a circle
mcqs.why: Centrifugal force is a fictitious apparent force that appears to act on a body moving in a circle.

mcqs.q: In which direction does centrifugal force appear to act?
options: Away from the centre, along the radius
