mcqs.why: Centrifugal force is directed away from the centre, along the radius, opposite to centripetal force.

mcqs.q: How does centrifugal force compare in magnitude to centripetal force?
options: It is equal in magnitude to the centripetal force
mcqs.why: Centrifugal force is equal in magnitude to the centripetal force but directed away from the centre.

mcqs.q: When does centrifugal force exist?
options: Only as long as the body moves in the circle
Even when the body is at rest
At all times for every body
mcqs.why: Centrifugal force exists only as long as the body moves in the circle, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Why do passengers in a bus taking a turn feel thrown outwards?
options: Because of a real outward gravity
They feel thrown outwards, away from the centre of the turn, the apparent centrifugal effect
mcqs.why: Passengers in a bus taking a turn feel thrown outwards, away from the centre of the turn, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: What provides the centripetal force for a whirled stone?
mcqs.why: The tension in the string keeps a whirled stone moving in its circular path, providing the centripetal force.

mcqs.q: What provides the centripetal force for a car taking a turn?
options: Gravity keeping the Moon in orbit
Friction between tyres and road, with banking of roads helping to provide it safely
mcqs.why: Friction between tyres and road provides centripetal force for a turning car, and banking of roads helps provide it safely.

mcqs.q: What provides the centripetal force keeping the Moon in its orbit?
mcqs.why: The Earth's gravity provides the centripetal force keeping the Moon in its orbit around the Earth.

mcqs.q: An aeroplane moves in a circle of radius 25 km at 270 km/h. Convert its speed to m/s.
mcqs.why: To convert km/h to m/s divide by 3.6: v = 270 / 3.6 = 75 m/s, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: For that aeroplane, with v = 75 m/s and r = 25000 m, what is the centripetal acceleration?
mcqs.why: ac = v squared / r = 75 squared / 25000 = 5625 / 25000 = 0.225 m/s squared.

lessons.title: Work and Its Units
lessons.notes_html:
Work is said to be done on an object when a force acts on it and produces a displacement in the direction of the applied force.

W = F × d

  • W — work done (J)
  • F — applied force (N)
  • d — displacement in the direction of the force (m)
  • If the force acts at an angle θ to the displacement, W = F d cos θ.
  • Work is maximum when force and displacement are parallel (θ = 0 degrees) and zero when they are perpendicular (θ = 90 degrees).

Unit of Work

The SI unit of work is the joule (J): one joule is the work done when a force of one newton displaces an object through one metre in its own direction.

Worked Example: Work Done by a Force

A force of 150 N is applied on a box and the box covers a distance of 7.5 m in the direction of the force. Calculate the work done.

Step 1: W = F × d (force and displacement in the same direction).

Step 2: W = 150 × 7.5 = 1125 J.

Answer: 1125 J

Worked Example: Work at an Angle

A body is pushed with a force of 500 N at an angle of 60 degrees with the horizontal. The body covers a distance of 10 m. How much work is done?

Step 1: W = F d cos θ

Step 2: W = 500 × 10 × cos 60 degrees = 5000 × 0.5 = 2500 J.

Answer: 2500 J

mcqs.q: Work is said to be done on an object when:
options: A force acts on it and produces a displacement in the direction of the force
A force acts on it but it does not move at all
It moves without any force acting on it
A force acts perpendicular to its motion only
mcqs.why: By definition, work needs a force and a displacement in the direction of the applied force, W = F x d.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for work done when force and displacement are in the same direction?
mcqs.why: Work is force times displacement in its direction: W = F x d, with F in newtons and d in metres.

mcqs.q: What is the SI unit of work?
mcqs.why: The SI unit of work is the joule (J). One joule is the work of one newton acting through one metre.

mcqs.q: One joule is the work done when:
options: A force of 1 N displaces an object through 10 m
A force of 10 N displaces an object through 1 m
A force of 1 N displaces an object through 1 m in its own direction
A force of 1 N acts for 1 second
mcqs.why: By definition 1 J = 1 N x 1 m = 1, the work of a one-newton force moving an object one metre.

mcqs.q: A force of 150 N moves a box 7.5 m in the direction of the force. The work done is:
mcqs.why: W = F x d = 150 x 7.5 = 1125 J, using the worked example values from the notes.

mcqs.q: If a force F acts at an angle theta to the displacement d, the work done is:
mcqs.why: Only the component of force along the displacement does work, so W = F d cos theta as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: Work done is maximum when the angle between force and displacement is:
mcqs.why: W = F d cos theta is largest when cos theta = 1, which happens at theta = 0 degrees, force parallel to displacement.

mcqs.q: Work done is zero when the force is perpendicular to the displacement, that is when theta equals:
mcqs.why: W = F d cos 90 degrees = F d x 0 = 0 J, so a perpendicular force does no work on the object.

mcqs.q: A body is pushed with 500 N at 60 degrees to the horizontal over 10 m. The work done is:
mcqs.why: W = F d cos theta = 500 x 10 x cos 60 degrees = 5000 x 0.5 = 2500 J, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: A force of 20 N moves an object 5 m in the direction of the force. The work done is:
mcqs.why: W = F x d = 20 x 5 = 100 J. Force in newtons times displacement in metres gives work in joules.

lessons.title: Energy, Its Forms and Interconversion
lessons.notes_html:
Energy is the capacity of a body to do work. We need energy for everything we do: moving, lifting, heating, lighting, and running machines and vehicles. Without energy, no work and no activity is possible. Energy is measured in joules (J).

Forms of Energy

  • Kinetic energy — due to motion.
  • Potential energy — due to position or configuration.
  • Chemical energy — stored in fuels and food.
  • Heat, light, sound and electrical energy.

Interconversion of Energy

Energy changes from one form into another: in a torch, chemical energy becomes electrical energy and then light and heat; in a dam, the potential energy of stored water becomes kinetic energy and then electrical energy. Energy is never created or destroyed in these changes; it is only converted.

mcqs.q: Energy is defined as:
options: The capacity of a body to do work
The product of mass and velocity
mcqs.why: Energy is the capacity of a body to do work. Without energy, no work and no activity is possible.

mcqs.q: Energy is measured in:
mcqs.why: Energy is measured in joules (J), the same unit as work, because energy is the capacity to do work.

mcqs.q: Kinetic energy is the energy a body has:
mcqs.why: Kinetic energy is due to motion, while potential energy is due to position or configuration, as listed in the notes.

mcqs.q: Potential energy is the energy a body has:
options: Due to its position or configuration
mcqs.why: Potential energy is due to position or configuration, unlike kinetic energy which is due to motion.

mcqs.q: Chemical energy is:
options: Energy stored in fuels and food
mcqs.why: Chemical energy is stored in fuels and food, and it is released and converted when the fuel or food is used.

mcqs.q: In a torch, the energy changes are:
options: Chemical becomes electrical, then light and heat
mcqs.why: In a torch, chemical energy of the cells becomes electrical energy and then light and heat, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: In a dam, the energy changes are:
options: Potential energy of stored water becomes kinetic energy and then electrical energy
Electrical energy becomes potential energy only
Kinetic energy becomes chemical energy only
mcqs.why: Stored water has potential energy; falling water has kinetic energy, which is then converted into electrical energy.

mcqs.q: During interconversion of energy, energy is:
options: Never created or destroyed, only converted
mcqs.why: Energy is never created or destroyed in these changes; it is only converted from one form into another.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a form of energy listed in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes list kinetic, potential, chemical, heat, light, sound and electrical energy as forms of energy.

mcqs.q: We need energy for activities such as:
options: Moving, lifting, heating, lighting and running machines
mcqs.why: The notes state we need energy for everything we do: moving, lifting, heating, lighting, and running machines and vehicles.

lessons.title: Kinetic Energy
lessons.notes_html:
Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by an object due to its motion. Running water and a moving car possess kinetic energy.

KE = 1/2 m v2

  • m — mass of the object (kg)
  • v — velocity of the object (m s-1)
  • Kinetic energy can never be negative: mass is always positive and v2 is always positive, so KE is zero at rest and positive in motion.
  • If the velocity is doubled, KE becomes four times; if it is tripled, KE becomes nine times.

Derivation of the Formula

Step 1: Work done on a body starting from rest = F × S = m × a × S.

Step 2: From the third equation of motion, with vi = 0: 2aS = v2, so a × S = v2 / 2.

Step 3: Work done = m × v2 / 2. This work is stored as kinetic energy, so KE = 1/2 m v2.

Worked Example: Kinetic Energy of a Runner

The mass of a girl is 45 kg. If she is running at 10 m s-1, calculate her kinetic energy.

Step 1: KE = 1/2 m v2

Step 2: KE = 0.5 × 45 × 102 = 0.5 × 45 × 100 = 2250 J.

Answer: 2250 J

Worked Example: Speed from Kinetic Energy

The mass of a car is 800 kg. Calculate the speed of the car if its kinetic energy is 2.5 × 105 J.

Step 1: From KE = 1/2 m v2, v2 = 2 × KE / m.

Step 2: v2 = 2 × 2.5 × 105 / 800 = 500,000 / 800 = 625.

Step 3: v = 25 m s-1.

Answer: 25 m s-1

mcqs.q: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by an object due to:
mcqs.why: Kinetic energy is due to motion. Running water and a moving car possess kinetic energy, as the notes state.

mcqs.q: The formula for kinetic energy is:
mcqs.why: KE = 1/2 m v^2, where m is mass in kg and v is velocity in m/s. The work done starting from rest gives this result.

mcqs.q: A girl of mass 45 kg runs at 10 m/s. Her kinetic energy is:
mcqs.why: KE = 1/2 m v^2 = 0.5 x 45 x 10^2 = 0.5 x 45 x 100 = 2250 J, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: Kinetic energy can never be negative because:
options: Mass is always positive and v^2 is always positive
Velocity is squared and becomes negative
mcqs.why: Mass is always positive and v^2 is always positive, so KE is zero at rest and positive in motion, never negative.

mcqs.q: If the velocity of a body is doubled, its kinetic energy becomes:
mcqs.why: KE = 1/2 m v^2 depends on v squared: (2v)^2 = 4v^2, so doubling velocity makes KE four times larger.

mcqs.q: If the velocity of a body is tripled, its kinetic energy becomes:
mcqs.why: KE varies as v^2: (3v)^2 = 9v^2, so tripling the velocity makes the kinetic energy nine times larger.

mcqs.q: A car of mass 800 kg has kinetic energy 2.5 x 10^5 J. Its speed is:
mcqs.why: v^2 = 2 x KE / m = 2 x 2.5 x 10^5 / 800 = 500000 / 800 = 625, so v = 25 m/s, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: The kinetic energy of a body at rest is:
mcqs.why: At rest v = 0, so KE = 1/2 m x 0^2 = 0 J. Kinetic energy is zero at rest and positive in motion.

mcqs.q: In the derivation of KE, work done on a body starting from rest equals:
options: F x S = m x a x S
mcqs.why: Step 1 of the derivation: work = F x S = m x a x S, and with 2aS = v^2 this gives KE = 1/2 m v^2.

mcqs.q: A body of mass 2 kg moves at 3 m/s. Its kinetic energy is:
mcqs.why: KE = 1/2 m v^2 = 0.5 x 2 x 3^2 = 1 x 9 = 9 J, applying the formula KE = 1/2 m v^2 directly.

lessons.title: Potential Energy
lessons.notes_html:
Potential energy is the energy possessed by an object due to its position or configuration (shape or size). Examples: water stored in a dam, a ball held above the ground, and a stretched or compressed spring (elastic potential energy).

Gravitational Potential Energy

Gravitational potential energy is the energy possessed by an object due to its height above the surface of the Earth.

PE = m × g × h

  • m — mass (kg)
  • g — acceleration due to gravity (m s-2)
  • h — height above the chosen reference level (m)

Derivation

Step 1: To lift a mass m slowly through a height h, the lifting force must equal the weight, F = m × g.

Step 2: Work done = F × h = m × g × h.

Step 3: This work is stored in the body as gravitational potential energy, so PE = mgh.

Worked Example: Potential Energy at Two Heights

An object has a mass of 25 kg. Calculate its potential energy (a) 5 m above the ground, (b) 10 m above the ground. Take g = 9.8 m s-2.

Step 1: PE = m × g × h

Step 2: (a) PE = 25 × 9.8 × 5 = 1225 J.

Step 3: (b) PE = 25 × 9.8 × 10 = 2450 J.

Answer: (a) 1225 J, (b) 2450 J

mcqs.q: Potential energy is the energy possessed by an object due to:
mcqs.why: Potential energy is due to position or configuration (shape or size), for example water stored in a dam.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of potential energy in the notes?
mcqs.why: Water stored in a dam, a ball held above the ground, and a stretched spring are the potential energy examples given.

mcqs.q: The energy of a stretched or compressed spring is called:
mcqs.why: A stretched or compressed spring stores elastic potential energy because of its changed configuration.

mcqs.q: Gravitational potential energy is due to an object's:
options: Height above the surface of the Earth
mcqs.why: Gravitational potential energy is the energy due to height above the surface of the Earth, PE = m x g x h.

mcqs.q: The formula for gravitational potential energy is:
options: PE = F x d cos theta
PE = m x g x h
mcqs.why: PE = m x g x h, where m is mass, g is acceleration due to gravity and h is height above the reference level.

mcqs.q: An object of mass 25 kg is 5 m above the ground (g = 9.8 m/s^2). Its potential energy is:
mcqs.why: PE = m x g x h = 25 x 9.8 x 5 = 1225 J, exactly as calculated in the worked example in the notes.

mcqs.q: The same 25 kg object at 10 m above the ground (g = 9.8 m/s^2) has potential energy:
mcqs.why: PE = m x g x h = 25 x 9.8 x 10 = 2450 J. Doubling the height doubles the potential energy.

mcqs.q: In the derivation of PE = mgh, the lifting force must equal:
options: The weight, F = m x g
mcqs.why: To lift mass m slowly, the lifting force equals the weight F = m x g, so work = F x h = m x g x h = PE.

mcqs.q: In PE = mgh, h is measured from:
options: The centre of the Earth always
The top of the object only
mcqs.why: h is the height above the chosen reference level, as defined with the formula PE = m x g x h in the notes.

mcqs.q: A mass of 10 kg is lifted 2 m (g = 9.8 m/s^2). The gain in potential energy is:
mcqs.why: PE = m x g x h = 10 x 9.8 x 2 = 196 J. The work done in lifting is stored as gravitational potential energy.

lessons.title: Dissipation and Conservation of Energy
lessons.notes_html:
Dissipation of Energy

In every real energy conversion, a part of the energy is wasted — spread out as heat, sound and friction — and cannot be recovered for useful work. This loss is called dissipation of energy.

Principle of Conservation of Energy

Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be changed from one form into another. The total energy of an isolated system always remains the same. For example, when a ball falls, its potential energy changes into kinetic energy; just before it lands, PE lost = KE gained (if air friction is ignored).

Perpetual Machines

A perpetual machine — a machine that runs forever without any energy input and keeps giving out useful work — is not possible. In every conversion some energy is lost as heat and friction, so the output is always less than the input and the machine must eventually stop.

mcqs.q: Dissipation of energy means:
options: Part of the energy is wasted as heat, sound and friction and cannot be recovered
Energy disappears and total energy increases
mcqs.why: In every real conversion part of the energy is spread out as heat, sound and friction and cannot be recovered for useful work.

mcqs.q: The principle of conservation of energy states that energy:
options: Can neither be created nor destroyed, only changed in form
Can be created but not destroyed
Can be destroyed but not created
mcqs.why: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only change form, and the total energy of an isolated system stays the same.

mcqs.q: When a ball falls (ignoring air friction), just before it lands:
options: Both PE and KE are lost
mcqs.why: As the ball falls its potential energy changes into kinetic energy, so PE lost = KE gained if air friction is ignored.

mcqs.q: The total energy of an isolated system:
mcqs.why: By conservation of energy, the total energy of an isolated system always remains the same; only its form changes.

mcqs.q: A perpetual machine is a machine that:
options: Runs forever without any energy input and keeps giving out useful work
mcqs.why: A perpetual machine would run forever with no energy input while giving useful work out, which the notes say is not possible.

mcqs.q: A perpetual machine is not possible because:
options: Energy is created in every conversion
In every conversion some energy is lost as heat and friction, so output is less than input
mcqs.why: Some energy is always lost as heat and friction, so output is always less than input and the machine must eventually stop.

mcqs.q: In a real energy conversion, the useful output is:
mcqs.why: Because part of the energy is dissipated as heat and friction, the useful output is always less than the total input.

mcqs.q: Dissipated energy is spread out mainly as:
mcqs.why: The wasted part of the energy is spread out as heat, sound and friction and cannot be recovered for useful work.

mcqs.q: As a falling ball loses height, its energy change is:
options: Kinetic energy changes into potential energy
Potential energy changes into kinetic energy
mcqs.why: When a ball falls, its potential energy changes into kinetic energy, keeping the total energy the same.

mcqs.q: Why must a so-called perpetual machine eventually stop?
options: Its output is less than its input due to losses, so it runs out of usable energy
mcqs.why: Losses as heat and friction make output less than input in every cycle, so without fresh input the machine must stop.

lessons.title: Major Sources and Non-Renewable Sources
lessons.notes_html:
Major Sources of Energy

  • Fossil fuels (coal, oil and natural gas)
  • Solar energy
  • Wind energy
  • Hydroelectric energy
  • Geothermal energy
  • Biomass and biogas
  • Nuclear energy
  • Tidal and sea energy

Non-Renewable Sources

Non-renewable sources cannot be replenished in a short duration of time. Fossil fuels were formed from dead plants and animals over millions of years under the Earth, and they are being used up far faster than nature can replace them.

  • Fossil fuels — coal, oil and natural gas: burnt for heat, transport and electricity.
  • Nuclear fuel (uranium) — releases a very large amount of energy from a small mass in nuclear power stations.

mcqs.q: Which of these is listed as a major source of energy?
mcqs.why: Major sources listed are fossil fuels, solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, biomass and biogas, nuclear, and tidal energy.

mcqs.q: Non-renewable sources of energy are those that:
options: Can be used again and again
Are replenished in a short time
Cannot be replenished in a short duration of time
mcqs.why: Non-renewable sources cannot be replenished in a short duration of time, unlike renewable sources which refill quickly.

mcqs.q: Fossil fuels are:
mcqs.why: The fossil fuels are coal, oil and natural gas, burnt for heat, transport and electricity as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Fossil fuels were formed:
options: From dead plants and animals over millions of years under the Earth
From seawater in a few days
mcqs.why: Fossil fuels formed from dead plants and animals over millions of years under the Earth, so they cannot be replaced quickly.

mcqs.q: Fossil fuels are being used up:
options: At the same rate nature replaces them
Far faster than nature can replace them
mcqs.why: They are being used up far faster than nature can replace them, which is why they are classed as non-renewable.

mcqs.q: Fossil fuels are burnt for:
mcqs.why: The notes state fossil fuels — coal, oil and natural gas — are burnt for heat, transport and electricity.

mcqs.q: The nuclear fuel named in the notes is:
mcqs.why: Nuclear fuel (uranium) releases energy in nuclear power stations. It is listed with the non-renewable sources.

mcqs.q: Nuclear fuel is notable because it releases:
options: A very small amount of energy from a large mass
A very large amount of energy from a small mass
mcqs.why: Uranium releases a very large amount of energy from a small mass in nuclear power stations, as the notes state.

mcqs.q: Which pair are both major sources of energy in the notes?
mcqs.why: Wind energy and hydroelectric energy are both in the major sources list, along with solar, geothermal and others.

mcqs.q: Tidal and sea energy is listed among:
mcqs.why: Tidal and sea energy appears in the major sources list together with solar, wind, hydroelectric and nuclear energy.

lessons.title: Renewable Sources of Energy
lessons.notes_html:
Renewable sources of energy can be used again and again, or are replenished in a short span of time.

  • Biofuels — chemical energy stored in plants and animal waste (biomass and biogas).
  • Hydroelectric resources — energy from running or falling water: water stored behind a dam falls on turbines, and its kinetic energy is converted into electrical energy by generators.
  • Solar radiation — energy from the Sun, used in solar panels and solar heaters.
  • Geothermal resources — heat from inside the Earth.
  • Wind energy — the kinetic energy of blowing air, converted by windmills and wind turbines into mechanical and then electrical energy.
  • Energy from the sea — tides, caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon on the Earth's oceans, and waves.

Solar Panels: Uses and Balance

  • Uses: producing electricity for homes, schools and street lights; heating water in solar geysers; running water pumps in fields; charging batteries and running calculators and remote installations.
  • Advantages: free, renewable, pollution-free and available almost everywhere.
  • Disadvantages: available only in daytime and fair weather; panels and storage batteries are costly; a large area is needed for large-scale generation.

mcqs.q: Renewable sources of energy are those that:
options: Cannot be replenished in a short time
Can be used again and again, or are replenished in a short span of time
Are formed over millions of years
mcqs.why: Renewable sources can be used again and again, or are replenished in a short span of time, unlike fossil fuels.

mcqs.q: Biofuels store chemical energy in:
options: Plants and animal waste (biomass and biogas)
mcqs.why: Biofuels are chemical energy stored in plants and animal waste, that is biomass and biogas, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: In hydroelectric generation, water stored behind a dam:
options: Falls on turbines and its kinetic energy becomes electrical energy by generators
mcqs.why: Falling water drives turbines, and its kinetic energy is converted into electrical energy by generators.

mcqs.q: Geothermal resources are:
mcqs.why: Geothermal resources are heat from inside the Earth, listed separately from solar, wind and sea energy.

mcqs.q: Wind energy is:
options: The potential energy of stored water
The kinetic energy of blowing air
mcqs.why: Wind energy is the kinetic energy of blowing air, converted by windmills and turbines into mechanical then electrical energy.

mcqs.q: Tides are caused mainly by:
options: The gravitational pull of the Moon on the Earth's oceans
mcqs.why: Energy from the sea includes tides, caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon on the Earth's oceans, and waves.

mcqs.q: Solar panels can be used for:
options: Producing electricity for homes, schools and street lights
mcqs.why: Uses listed: electricity for homes, schools and street lights; solar geysers; field pumps; charging batteries and calculators.

mcqs.q: An advantage of solar energy is that it is:
options: Free, renewable, pollution-free and available almost everywhere
Available only in fair weather at night
mcqs.why: Advantages given: free, renewable, pollution-free and available almost everywhere. Fuel costs nothing for solar energy.

mcqs.q: A disadvantage of solar energy is that it is:
options: Available only in daytime and fair weather
mcqs.why: Disadvantages given: available only in daytime and fair weather; panels and batteries are costly; large area is needed.

mcqs.q: Windmills and wind turbines convert wind energy into:
options: Chemical and then heat energy only
mcqs.why: The kinetic energy of blowing air is converted by windmills and wind turbines into mechanical and then electrical energy.

lessons.title: Efficiency
lessons.notes_html:
The efficiency of a system is the ratio of the useful energy (or work) output to the total energy (or work) input, usually expressed as a percentage. It tells how much of the input energy is actually converted into useful form; the rest is lost, usually as heat.

Efficiency = useful output / total input × 100%

  • Efficiency is always less than 100%, because some energy is always lost in every conversion.

mcqs.q: Efficiency of a system is defined as:
options: Total input divided by useful output
Useful energy output divided by total energy input
Useful output multiplied by total input
Total input minus useful output only
mcqs.why: Efficiency = useful output / total input, usually expressed as a percentage. It shows how much input becomes useful.

mcqs.q: The formula for efficiency as a percentage is:
options: Efficiency = useful output / total input x 100%
Efficiency = total input / useful output x 100%
Efficiency = useful output + total input x 100%
Efficiency = useful output x total input x 100%
mcqs.why: Efficiency = useful output / total input x 100%. The rest of the input is lost, usually as heat.

mcqs.q: A machine takes 100 J input and gives 80 J useful output. Its efficiency is:
mcqs.why: Efficiency = useful output / total input x 100% = 80 / 100 x 100% = 80%. The remaining 20 J is lost.

mcqs.q: A device takes 200 J input and gives 150 J useful output. Its efficiency is:
mcqs.why: Efficiency = useful output / total input x 100% = 150 / 200 x 100% = 75%. So 50 J of the input is wasted.

mcqs.q: Efficiency is always less than 100% because:
options: Some energy is always lost in every conversion
mcqs.why: Efficiency is always less than 100% because some energy is always lost in every conversion, usually as heat.

mcqs.q: The part of the input energy that is not converted into useful form is usually lost as:
mcqs.why: Efficiency tells how much input becomes useful; the rest is lost, usually as heat, so efficiency stays below 100%.

mcqs.q: A motor takes 90 J input and gives 45 J useful output. Its efficiency is:
mcqs.why: Efficiency = useful output / total input x 100% = 45 / 90 x 100% = 50%. Half the input is converted usefully.

mcqs.q: A system has efficiency 25% and total input 400 J. Its useful output is:
mcqs.why: Useful output = efficiency x total input = 0.25 x 400 = 100 J. Check: 100 / 400 x 100% = 25% efficiency.

mcqs.q: A system gives 60 J useful output from 120 J input. Its efficiency is:
mcqs.why: Efficiency = useful output / total input x 100% = 60 / 120 x 100% = 50%. The other 60 J is lost, usually as heat.

mcqs.q: Efficiency tells us:
options: How much of the input energy is actually converted into useful form
The total energy created by a system
The power of a system in watts
mcqs.why: It tells how much of the input energy is actually converted into useful form; the rest is lost, usually as heat.

lessons.title: Power and Its Units
lessons.notes_html:
Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is consumed.

P = W / t

  • P — power (W)
  • W — work done (J)
  • t — time taken (s)

Units of Power

  • The SI unit of power is the watt (W): one watt is the power which does one joule of work in one second, 1 W = 1 J s-1.
  • One horsepower (hp) = 746 W.

Worked Example: Power of a Crane

A crane lifts a load weighing 3000 N through a height of 5 m in 10 seconds. What is the power of the crane in hp?

Step 1: Work done W = 3000 × 5 = 15,000 J.

Step 2: Power P = W / t = 15,000 / 10 = 1500 W.

Step 3: In hp, P = 1500 / 746 = 2.01, about 2 hp.

Answer: about 2 hp

Key Points

  • Work = force × displacement in the direction of the force; unit joule.
  • KE = 1/2 mv2; gravitational PE = mgh.
  • Energy is conserved: it changes form but is never created or destroyed.
  • Power = work / time; unit watt; 1 hp = 746 W.
  • Efficiency is always less than 100%.

mcqs.q: Power is defined as:
options: The rate at which work is done or energy is consumed
mcqs.why: Power is the rate of doing work or consuming energy: P = W / t, with work in joules and time in seconds.

mcqs.q: The formula for power is:
mcqs.why: P = W / t, where P is power in watts, W is work done in joules and t is time taken in seconds.

mcqs.q: The SI unit of power is:
mcqs.why: The SI unit of power is the watt (W): one watt does one joule of work in one second, 1 W = 1 J/s.

mcqs.q: One watt is the power which:
options: Does 1 J of work in 1 second
Does 10 J of work in 1 second
Does 1 J of work in 10 seconds
mcqs.why: 1 W = 1 J s^-1: one watt is the power which does one joule of work in one second, as defined in the notes.

mcqs.q: One horsepower (hp) is equal to:
mcqs.why: One horsepower (hp) = 746 W. This conversion is used to express the crane power of 1500 W as about 2 hp.

mcqs.q: A crane lifts a 3000 N load through 5 m. The work done is:
mcqs.why: W = F x d = 3000 x 5 = 15000 J. This is step 1 of the crane worked example in the notes.

mcqs.q: The crane does 15000 J of work in 10 s. Its power is:
mcqs.why: P = W / t = 15000 / 10 = 1500 W. Power is work divided by time, giving watts when work is in joules.

mcqs.q: The crane power of 1500 W is about:
mcqs.why: P in hp = 1500 / 746 = 2.01, about 2 hp, since one horsepower equals 746 watts as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: A machine does 600 J of work in 20 s. Its power is:
mcqs.why: P = W / t = 600 / 20 = 30 W. Dividing joules by seconds gives the power in watts directly.

mcqs.q: In P = W / t, the symbols W and t stand for:
options: W is weight and t is temperature
W is work done (J) and t is time taken (s)
W is watt and t is torque
W is width and t is thickness
mcqs.why: P is power (W), W is work done (J) and t is time taken (s), exactly as labelled with the formula in the notes.

lessons.title: Pressure
lessons.notes_html:
Pressure is the force per unit area applied perpendicularly on the surface of an object.

P = F / A

  • P — pressure (Pa)
  • F — force acting perpendicular to the surface (N)
  • A — area over which the force acts (m2)
  • The SI unit of pressure is the newton per square metre (N m-2), called the pascal: 1 Pa = 1 N m-2. The bar is another unit of pressure.
  • Pressure increases when the force increases or the area decreases.

Pressure in Daily Life

  • A sharp knife cuts easily: its edge has a very small area, so the same force produces a much larger pressure. A blunt knife spreads the force over a larger area and cannot cut.
  • Broad tyres are used in tractors: they spread the weight over a larger area, so the pressure on soft ground is smaller and the tractor does not sink.
  • Footprints are left in sand because the body's weight acts on the small area of the foot, producing a pressure the sand cannot support.
  • A rubber sucker sticks to a smooth surface: pressing it pushes the air out, and the greater atmospheric pressure outside holds it firmly.

Worked Example: Pressure on a Nail

A hammer exerts a force of 2.5 N on a nail of tip area 1 mm2. Calculate the pressure on the nail.

Step 1: Convert area: 1 mm2 = 1 × 10-6 m2.

Step 2: Pressure = F / A = 2.5 / (1 × 10-6) = 2.5 × 106 N m-2.

Answer: 2.5 × 106 N m-2

Worked Example: Maximum and Minimum Pressure

The length, breadth and height of a rectangular wooden block are 60 cm, 30 cm and 15 cm. Its mass is 13.5 kg and it is placed on a table. Calculate the maximum and minimum pressure exerted by the block. Take g = 9.8 m s-2.

Step 1: Weight = 13.5 × 9.8 = 132.3 N.

Step 2: The three face areas are 0.60 × 0.30 = 0.18 m2, 0.60 × 0.15 = 0.09 m2 and 0.30 × 0.15 = 0.045 m2.

Step 3: Maximum pressure is on the smallest face: 132.3 / 0.045 = 2940 Pa.

Step 4: Minimum pressure is on the largest face: 132.3 / 0.18 = 735 Pa.

Answer: maximum 2940 Pa; minimum 735 Pa

mcqs.q: Pressure is defined as:
options: Force per unit area applied perpendicularly on a surface
mcqs.why: Pressure = force / area, where the force acts perpendicularly on the surface: P = F / A, measured in pascals.

mcqs.q: The formula for pressure is:
mcqs.why: P = F / A, where F is the perpendicular force in newtons and A is the area in square metres.

mcqs.q: The SI unit of pressure, the pascal, equals:
mcqs.why: 1 Pa = 1 N m^-2, the newton per square metre. The bar is another unit of pressure mentioned in the notes.

mcqs.q: Pressure increases when:
options: Force and area both decrease equally
mcqs.why: From P = F / A, pressure increases when the force increases or the area decreases, and falls in the opposite cases.

mcqs.q: A sharp knife cuts easily because:
options: Its edge has a large area
Its edge has a very small area, so the same force gives a much larger pressure
It is heavier than a blunt knife
mcqs.why: A sharp edge has a very small area, so P = F / A is much larger for the same force and it cuts easily.

mcqs.q: Broad tyres are used in tractors so that:
options: Pressure on soft ground is larger and the tractor grips
Weight is spread over a larger area, pressure is smaller, and the tractor does not sink
mcqs.why: Broad tyres spread the weight over a larger area, so P = F / A on soft ground is smaller and the tractor does not sink.

mcqs.q: A hammer exerts 2.5 N on a nail of tip area 1 mm^2 (1 x 10^-6 m^2). The pressure is:
mcqs.why: P = F / A = 2.5 / (1 x 10^-6) = 2.5 x 10^6 N/m^2, exactly as in the worked example in the notes.

mcqs.q: A 13.5 kg block weighs (g = 9.8 m/s^2):
mcqs.why: Weight = m x g = 13.5 x 9.8 = 132.3 N. This weight is the force used for the block pressure calculations.

mcqs.q: For the block (faces 0.18, 0.09, 0.045 m^2, weight 132.3 N), maximum pressure is:
mcqs.why: Maximum pressure is on the smallest face: P = F / A = 132.3 / 0.045 = 2940 Pa, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: For the same block, minimum pressure is:
mcqs.why: Minimum pressure is on the largest face: P = F / A = 132.3 / 0.18 = 735 Pa, as in the worked example.

lessons.title: Atmospheric Pressure and Its Applications
lessons.notes_html:
Atmospheric pressure is the force per unit area exerted on a surface by the weight of the air column above that surface in the atmosphere of the Earth.

  • At sea level it is about 1.013 × 105 N m-2, equal to the pressure of a 76 cm (760 mm) column of mercury.
  • The atmosphere exerts equal pressure in all directions.
  • A rapid increase in atmospheric pressure indicates clear, pleasant weather; a sudden fall usually brings rain, storm or poor weather.

Applications of Atmospheric Pressure

  • A rubber sucker sticks to a wall because the outside air pressure holds it.
  • Drinking through a straw: sucking lowers the pressure inside the straw and atmospheric pressure pushes the liquid up.
  • A syringe fills when its piston is pulled back.
  • A barometer measures atmospheric pressure to forecast weather.

mcqs.q: Atmospheric pressure is:
options: Force per unit area exerted by the weight of the air column above a surface
Pressure at the centre of the Earth
mcqs.why: It is the force per unit area exerted on a surface by the weight of the air column above it in the atmosphere.

mcqs.q: At sea level, atmospheric pressure is about:
mcqs.why: At sea level it is about 1.013 x 10^5 N/m^2, equal to the pressure of a 76 cm column of mercury.

mcqs.q: Atmospheric pressure at sea level equals the pressure of a mercury column of height:
mcqs.why: It equals a 76 cm (760 mm) column of mercury. The 10.3 m figure is the equivalent water column height.

mcqs.q: The atmosphere exerts pressure:
mcqs.why: The atmosphere exerts equal pressure in all directions, which is why a rubber sucker is held from the outside.

mcqs.q: A rapid increase in atmospheric pressure indicates:
mcqs.why: A rapid increase indicates clear, pleasant weather; a sudden fall usually brings rain, storm or poor weather.

mcqs.q: A sudden fall in atmospheric pressure usually brings:
mcqs.why: A sudden fall usually brings rain, storm or poor weather, which is why barometer readings help forecast weather.

mcqs.q: Drinking through a straw works because:
options: Sucking lowers pressure in the straw and atmospheric pressure pushes the liquid up
mcqs.why: Sucking lowers the pressure inside the straw, and the greater atmospheric pressure outside pushes the liquid up.

mcqs.q: A rubber sucker sticks to a wall because:
options: The outside air pressure holds it after air is pushed out
mcqs.why: Pressing pushes the air out, and the greater atmospheric pressure outside holds the sucker firmly to the surface.

mcqs.q: A syringe fills when:
options: Its piston is pulled back and atmospheric pressure pushes liquid in
mcqs.why: Pulling the piston back lowers the inside pressure, so atmospheric pressure pushes the liquid into the syringe.

mcqs.q: A barometer is used to:
options: Measure atmospheric pressure to forecast weather
Measure the pressure of a gas supply only
mcqs.why: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure to forecast weather; rising pressure means clear weather, falling means rain.

lessons.title: Measuring Atmospheric Pressure: The Mercury Barometer
lessons.notes_html:
A barometer is the device used to measure atmospheric pressure. An altimeter uses the fall of pressure with height to measure altitude.

Mercury Barometer

A long glass tube, closed at one end, is filled with mercury and inverted in a reservoir of mercury. The mercury column falls until its pressure balances the atmospheric pressure pressing on the reservoir. At sea level the column stands about 76 cm high.

Why Mercury, Not Water?

Water cannot be used as a barometric liquid: its density is about 13.6 times smaller than mercury, so a water barometer would need a column about 10.3 m tall — far too tall for a practical instrument. Water also evaporates and sticks to glass, making readings unreliable.

Variation with Altitude

Atmospheric pressure is caused by the weight of the air above. As altitude increases, the column of air above becomes shorter and thinner, so its weight and the pressure fall: at an altitude of 30 km the pressure drops to about 10 mm of mercury, against 760 mm at sea level.

mcqs.q: A barometer is the device used to measure:
mcqs.why: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure. An altimeter uses the fall of pressure with height to measure altitude.

mcqs.q: An altimeter measures altitude by using:
options: The rise of temperature with height
The fall of pressure with height
mcqs.why: An altimeter uses the fall of pressure with height to measure altitude, since pressure drops as altitude increases.

mcqs.q: In a mercury barometer, the glass tube is:
options: Closed at one end, filled with mercury and inverted in a reservoir of mercury
mcqs.why: The tube is closed at one end, filled with mercury and inverted in a reservoir; the column balances atmospheric pressure.

mcqs.q: The mercury column stops falling when:
options: Its pressure balances the atmospheric pressure on the reservoir
mcqs.why: The column falls until its pressure balances the atmospheric pressure pressing on the reservoir surface.

mcqs.q: At sea level the mercury column stands about:
mcqs.why: At sea level the column stands about 76 cm high, corresponding to 1.013 x 10^5 Pa atmospheric pressure.

mcqs.q: Water is not used as a barometric liquid mainly because:
options: Its density is about 13.6 times smaller than mercury, needing a column about 10.3 m tall
mcqs.why: Water density is about 13.6 times smaller, so a water barometer needs a column about 10.3 m tall - impractical.

mcqs.q: Another reason water is unsuitable in a barometer is that it:
options: Evaporates and sticks to glass, making readings unreliable
mcqs.why: Water also evaporates and sticks to glass, making readings unreliable, in addition to needing a 10.3 m column.

mcqs.q: As altitude increases, atmospheric pressure:
options: Falls, because the air column above becomes shorter and thinner
mcqs.why: The column of air above becomes shorter and thinner with altitude, so its weight and the pressure fall.

mcqs.q: At an altitude of 30 km, atmospheric pressure drops to about:
mcqs.why: At 30 km the pressure drops to about 10 mm of mercury, against 760 mm at sea level, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: The space at the top of a mercury barometer tube (above the column) is:
options: Filled with air at high pressure
mcqs.why: The diagram labels the space above the mercury as vacuum, so only atmospheric pressure on the reservoir supports the column.

lessons.title: Pressure in Liquids
lessons.notes_html:
The pressure at a point inside a liquid increases with depth and with the density of the liquid, and it acts equally in all directions at the same depth.

P = ρ × g × h

  • P — pressure at the point (Pa)
  • ρ (rho) — density of the liquid (kg m-3)
  • g — acceleration due to gravity (m s-2)
  • h — depth of the point below the surface (m)

Worked Example: Pressure at the Bottom of a Reservoir

The depth of a domestic underground water reservoir is 2.5 m. Calculate the pressure exerted by water on the bottom of the reservoir. The density of water is 1 × 103 kg m-3.

Step 1: P = ρ × g × h = 1000 × 9.8 × 2.5 = 24,500 Pa.

Step 2: Pressure in a liquid acts equally in all directions, so at the same depth the pressure on the walls is the same; higher up the wall it is less, because it increases with depth.

Answer: 2.45 × 104 Pa

Worked Example: Height of a Water Column

What height of a vertical column of water will exert a pressure of 4.9 × 105 N m-2? The density of water is 1 × 103 kg m-3.

Step 1: h = P / (ρ × g)

Step 2: h = 4.9 × 105 / (1000 × 9.8) = 490,000 / 9800 = 50 m.

Answer: 50 m

mcqs.q: Pressure at a point inside a liquid increases with:
options: Depth and density of the liquid
mcqs.why: Liquid pressure increases with depth and with density, and acts equally in all directions at the same depth: P = rho g h.

mcqs.q: The formula for pressure in a liquid is:
options: P = rho x g x h
P = m x g x h
mcqs.why: P = rho x g x h, where rho is density in kg/m^3, g is acceleration due to gravity and h is depth in metres.

mcqs.q: At the same depth in a liquid, pressure acts:
mcqs.why: Pressure in a liquid acts equally in all directions at the same depth, so wall pressure equals bottom pressure at that depth.

mcqs.q: Water (density 1000 kg/m^3) fills a reservoir 2.5 m deep. Pressure at the bottom (g = 9.8) is:
mcqs.why: P = rho g h = 1000 x 9.8 x 2.5 = 24500 Pa = 2.45 x 10^4 Pa, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: Higher up the reservoir wall, the water pressure is:
options: The same as at the bottom
Less, because it increases with depth
mcqs.why: Pressure increases with depth, so higher up the wall (smaller h in P = rho g h) the pressure is less.

mcqs.q: What height of water column exerts 4.9 x 10^5 N/m^2 (density 1000, g = 9.8)?
mcqs.why: h = P / (rho x g) = 4.9 x 10^5 / (1000 x 9.8) = 490000 / 9800 = 50 m, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: In P = rho g h, rho stands for:
options: Density of the liquid in kg/m^3
mcqs.why: rho is the density of the liquid in kg/m^3, g is in m/s^2 and h is the depth below the surface in metres.

mcqs.q: If the depth in the same liquid is doubled, the liquid pressure:
mcqs.why: P = rho g h is directly proportional to h: doubling h gives P = rho g (2h) = 2 x rho g h, double the pressure.

mcqs.q: The pressure due to water at depth 1 m (density 1000, g = 9.8) is:
mcqs.why: P = rho g h = 1000 x 9.8 x 1 = 9800 Pa. Each metre of water depth adds 9800 Pa of pressure.

mcqs.q: Liquid pressure at a point does NOT depend on:
mcqs.why: P = rho g h depends only on density, g and depth - not on the container shape or total volume of liquid.

lessons.title: Manometer
lessons.notes_html:
A manometer measures the pressure of a gas (or the difference between two pressures). It is a U-shaped tube containing a liquid, usually mercury or water.

Construction

  • A U-tube is partly filled with the liquid.
  • One arm is connected to the gas whose pressure is to be measured; the other arm is open to the air, or connected to a second pressure.

How It Measures Pressure

  • If the gas pressure is greater than atmospheric pressure, it pushes the liquid down on its side and up on the open side.
  • The difference in the liquid levels (h) gives the extra pressure: extra pressure = ρ × g × h.
  • Gas pressure = atmospheric pressure + ρgh (or atmospheric pressure - ρgh if the gas pressure is smaller).

Applications

  • Measuring the pressure of gas in a container or gas supply.
  • Checking pressure differences in laboratories and in heating and ventilation systems.

mcqs.q: A manometer measures:
options: The pressure of a gas (or the difference between two pressures)
mcqs.why: A manometer measures the pressure of a gas, or the difference between two pressures, using a U-tube of liquid.

mcqs.q: A manometer consists of:
options: A U-shaped tube containing a liquid, usually mercury or water
A mercury reservoir and a long tube only
mcqs.why: It is a U-shaped tube partly filled with liquid, usually mercury or water, with one arm connected to the gas.

mcqs.q: In a manometer, one arm is connected to the gas and the other arm is:
options: Open to the air, or connected to a second pressure
mcqs.why: One arm connects to the gas whose pressure is measured; the other is open to the air or to a second pressure.

mcqs.q: If gas pressure is greater than atmospheric pressure, the liquid in the manometer:
options: Is pushed down on the gas side and up on the open side
mcqs.why: Greater gas pressure pushes the liquid down on its side and up on the open side; the level difference gives the extra pressure.

mcqs.q: The extra pressure shown by a manometer level difference h is:
options: Extra pressure = m x g x h
Extra pressure = rho x g x h
mcqs.why: Extra pressure = rho x g x h, the liquid-column pressure for the difference in levels h between the two arms.

mcqs.q: When gas pressure is greater than atmospheric, gas pressure equals:
options: Atmospheric pressure minus rho g h
Atmospheric pressure plus rho g h
mcqs.why: Gas pressure = atmospheric pressure + rho g h when the gas pressure is the larger of the two pressures.

mcqs.q: When gas pressure is smaller than atmospheric, gas pressure equals:
options: Atmospheric pressure plus rho g h
Atmospheric pressure minus rho g h
mcqs.why: Gas pressure = atmospheric pressure - rho g h if the gas pressure is smaller, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: A manometer is used for:
options: Measuring the pressure of gas in a container or gas supply
mcqs.why: Applications: measuring gas pressure in a container or supply, and checking pressure differences in labs and heating systems.

mcqs.q: Manometers are also used to check pressure differences in:
options: Laboratories and heating and ventilation systems
mcqs.why: They check pressure differences in laboratories and in heating and ventilation systems, besides gas containers.

mcqs.q: The liquids usually used in a manometer are:
mcqs.why: The U-tube usually contains mercury or water. The level difference h in that liquid gives extra pressure = rho g h.

lessons.title: Pascal's Law and Its Applications
lessons.notes_html:
Pascal's Law

The pressure applied to a completely enclosed liquid is transmitted without any loss to all other parts of the liquid and to the enclosing walls. In other words, pressure acts equally in all directions in an enclosed liquid.

Hydraulic Jack

A hydraulic jack works on Pascal's law. It has a small piston (pump) and a large piston connected by a liquid. A small force on the small piston creates a pressure that is transmitted equally to the large piston; because the large piston has a much larger area, it lifts a much larger load. Pumping the handle repeatedly raises heavy vehicles with little effort.

Other Applications of Pascal's Law

  • Hydraulic press — compresses and shapes materials with a huge force.
  • Hydraulic brakes — the pressure from the brake pedal is transmitted through brake fluid equally to all wheels.
  • Hydraulic lift — raises cars in workshops for repair.

Key Points

  • Pressure = force / area; unit pascal (Pa).
  • Atmospheric pressure at sea level = 1.013 × 105 Pa = 76 cm of mercury.
  • Pressure in a liquid: P = ρgh; it grows with depth and density.
  • Pascal's law is the working principle of all hydraulic machines.

mcqs.q: Pascal's law states that pressure applied to a completely enclosed liquid is:
options: Transmitted without any loss to all other parts of the liquid and to the walls
mcqs.why: Pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted without loss to all parts and walls; it acts equally in all directions.

mcqs.q: In an enclosed liquid, pressure acts:
mcqs.why: Pascal's law: pressure acts equally in all directions in an enclosed liquid, reaching every part and the walls.

mcqs.q: A hydraulic jack works on:
mcqs.why: A hydraulic jack works on Pascal's law: pressure is transmitted equally through the enclosed liquid to the large piston.

mcqs.q: A hydraulic jack has:
options: A small piston (pump) and a large piston connected by a liquid
mcqs.why: It has a small piston and a large piston connected by a liquid; pressure from the small piston reaches the large one.

mcqs.q: In a hydraulic jack, the large piston lifts a much larger load because:
options: The same pressure acts on its much larger area, giving a much larger force
mcqs.why: Pressure is transmitted equally, and force = pressure x area, so the much larger area of the large piston gives a much larger force.

mcqs.q: Pumping the handle of a hydraulic jack repeatedly:
options: Raises heavy vehicles with little effort
mcqs.why: Repeated pumping raises heavy vehicles with little effort, because a small force on the small piston lifts a large load.

mcqs.q: A hydraulic press is used to:
options: Compress and shape materials with a huge force
mcqs.why: The hydraulic press, an application of Pascal's law, compresses and shapes materials with a huge force.

mcqs.q: In hydraulic brakes, pressure from the brake pedal is:
options: Transmitted through brake fluid equally to all wheels
mcqs.why: Brake pedal pressure is transmitted through brake fluid equally to all wheels, applying Pascal's law.

mcqs.q: A hydraulic lift is used to:
options: Raise cars in workshops for repair
mcqs.why: A hydraulic lift raises cars in workshops for repair, using pressure transmitted through an enclosed liquid.

mcqs.q: Pascal's law is the working principle of:
mcqs.why: Key point in the notes: Pascal's law is the working principle of all hydraulic machines - jack, press, brakes and lift.

lessons.title: Deformation of Solids and Hooke's Law
lessons.notes_html:
A force applied to a solid object can produce a change in its size — its length, area or volume — and in its shape. This change in size and shape is called deformation of the solid. If the force is within the elastic limit, the object returns to its original size and shape when the force is removed; beyond it, the deformation becomes permanent.

Hooke's Law

The force needed to stretch or compress a spring by some distance is proportional to that distance, provided the applied force does not exceed the elastic limit of the spring.

F = k × x

  • F — deforming force (N)
  • x — extension (or compression) produced (m)
  • k — spring constant (N m-1)

Spring Constant

The spring constant k = F / x is the ratio of the deforming force to the resulting extension. It measures the stiffness of the spring: a stiffer spring has a larger spring constant. Its unit is newton per metre (N m-1).

Limitations of Hooke's Law

  • It holds only within the elastic limit (limit of proportionality) of the material.
  • Beyond that limit the extension is no longer proportional to the force, the material does not return fully to its original shape, and eventually it may break.
  • It applies to solids, not to liquids or gases.

mcqs.q: What is deformation of a solid?
options: A change in the colour of a solid when heated
A change in the size and shape of a solid produced by a force
The melting of a solid into a liquid
The breaking of a solid into small pieces
mcqs.why: A force applied to a solid can change its length, area or volume and its shape; this change in size and shape is called deformation of the solid.

mcqs.q: A solid is stretched by a force within its elastic limit and the force is then removed. What happens?
options: The solid returns to its original size and shape
mcqs.why: Within the elastic limit the object returns to its original size and shape when the force is removed; only beyond the elastic limit does the deformation become permanent.

mcqs.q: Hooke's law states that the force needed to stretch or compress a spring is:
options: Proportional to the extension produced, provided the elastic limit is not exceeded
Equal to the extension multiplied by the time taken
mcqs.why: Hooke's law: the force needed to stretch or compress a spring by some distance is proportional to that distance, provided the applied force does not exceed the elastic limit of the spring.

mcqs.q: In the formula F = k x, the symbol k stands for:
mcqs.why: In F = k x, F is the deforming force in newtons, x is the extension (or compression) in metres and k is the spring constant, measured in N/m.

mcqs.q: A spring has a spring constant of 50 N/m. What force is needed to stretch it by 0.10 m?
mcqs.why: F = k x = 50 x 0.10 = 5 N. By Hooke's law the force equals the spring constant multiplied by the extension.

mcqs.q: A force of 30 N stretches a spring by 0.15 m. The spring constant of the spring is:
mcqs.why: k = F / x = 30 / 0.15 = 200 N/m. The spring constant is the ratio of the deforming force to the resulting extension.

mcqs.q: Which of the following springs is the stiffest?
mcqs.why: The spring constant measures the stiffness of a spring: a stiffer spring has a larger spring constant, and 300 N/m is the largest value listed.

mcqs.q: A spring with spring constant 120 N/m is pulled by a force of 24 N. The extension produced is:
mcqs.why: x = F / k = 24 / 120 = 0.2 m. Rearranging Hooke's law F = k x gives the extension as the force divided by the spring constant.

mcqs.q: Hooke's law holds only:
options: Within the elastic limit of the material
mcqs.why: Hooke's law holds only within the elastic limit (limit of proportionality) of the material; it applies to solids, not to liquids or gases.

mcqs.q: If a spring is stretched beyond its elastic limit, what happens?
options: It always returns fully to its original shape
It does not return fully to its original shape and may eventually break
The extension stays proportional to the force
Its spring constant becomes zero at once
mcqs.why: Beyond the elastic limit the extension is no longer proportional to the force, the material does not return fully to its original shape, and eventually it may break.

lessons.title: Load-Extension Graph
lessons.notes_html:
For a spring within its elastic limit, the load-extension graph is an inclined straight line through the origin: extension increases in direct proportion to load, verifying Hooke's law. The slope of the line (load / extension) gives the spring constant k. The limit of proportionality is the point up to which the graph stays straight; beyond the elastic limit the graph curves away and the spring does not fully recover.

Worked Example: Spring Constant from Data

In an experiment with a spring, loads of 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5 and 3.0 N gave spring lengths of 200, 225, 250, 275, 300, 325 and 350 mm. Find the extensions, describe the graph, and calculate the spring constant.

Step 1: Extension = length - original length (200 mm): 0, 25, 50, 75, 100, 125, 150 mm.

Step 2: Plotted with load on the x-axis and extension on the y-axis, the points lie on a straight line through the origin: extension is directly proportional to load, so Hooke's law is obeyed in this range.

Step 3: k = load / extension = 0.5 N / 25 mm = 0.5 / 0.025 = 20 N m-1 (the same from any pair, e.g. 3.0 / 0.150 = 20 N m-1).

Answer: k = 20 N m-1

Worked Example: Using Hooke's Law

A spring has a spring constant of 200 N m-1. How much force will be needed to produce an extension of 25 cm in the spring?

Step 1: Convert extension: 25 cm = 0.25 m.

Step 2: F = k × x = 200 × 0.25 = 50 N.

Answer: 50 N

mcqs.q: For a spring within its elastic limit, the load-extension graph is:
options: A curve bending towards the load axis
An inclined straight line through the origin
A straight line parallel to the extension axis
mcqs.why: Within the elastic limit, extension increases in direct proportion to load, so the load-extension graph is an inclined straight line through the origin, verifying Hooke's law.

mcqs.q: The slope of a load-extension graph, taken as load divided by extension, gives:
options: The original length of the spring
The elastic limit of the spring
mcqs.why: The slope of the line (load / extension) gives the spring constant k, because k = F / x at every point on the straight part of the graph.

mcqs.q: In an experiment, a load of 0.5 N extends a spring by 25 mm. The spring constant is:
mcqs.why: Convert the extension: 25 mm = 0.025 m. Then k = load / extension = 0.5 / 0.025 = 20 N/m.

mcqs.q: A spring of original length 200 mm is stretched to a length of 300 mm by a load of 2.0 N. Its extension is:
mcqs.why: Extension = stretched length - original length = 300 - 200 = 100 mm. The extension is the increase in length, not the final length itself.

mcqs.q: For the same spring, a load of 3.0 N produces an extension of 0.150 m. Which calculation correctly checks the spring constant?
options: k = 3.0 / 0.150 = 20 N/m, the same value as from any other pair of readings
mcqs.why: k = load / extension = 3.0 / 0.150 = 20 N/m. Within the elastic limit the same spring constant is obtained from any pair of load and extension readings.

mcqs.q: The limit of proportionality is:
options: The load at which the spring breaks
The point up to which the load-extension graph stays straight
The point where the extension becomes zero
The maximum length the spring can reach
mcqs.why: The limit of proportionality is the point up to which the graph stays straight; beyond the elastic limit the graph curves away and the spring does not fully recover.

mcqs.q: A spring has a spring constant of 200 N/m. How much force is needed to produce an extension of 25 cm in the spring?
mcqs.why: Convert the extension: 25 cm = 0.25 m. Then F = k x = 200 x 0.25 = 50 N.

mcqs.q: Beyond the elastic limit, the load-extension graph:
options: Stays a straight line through the origin
Curves away, and the spring does not fully recover when unloaded
mcqs.why: Beyond the elastic limit the graph curves away from the straight line and the spring does not fully recover its original length when the load is removed.

mcqs.q: In the experiment the spring length increases from 250 mm to 275 mm when the load increases from 1.0 N to 1.5 N. The extra extension is:
mcqs.why: Extra extension = 275 - 250 = 25 mm. Each extra 0.5 N of load adds the same 25 mm of extension, showing that extension is directly proportional to load.

mcqs.q: If the load on a spring within its elastic limit is doubled, the extension:
mcqs.why: Within the elastic limit extension is directly proportional to load, so doubling the load doubles the extension; this is why the graph is a straight line through the origin.

lessons.title: Applications of Hooke's Law
lessons.notes_html:
• Spring balance or scale — measures weight or force, because the extension of its spring is proportional to the load.
  • Vehicle suspension systems and shock absorbers — springs are chosen by their spring constant to carry the load smoothly.
  • Spring mattresses — springs compress in proportion to the load on them.
  • Balance wheel of a mechanical watch — keeps the watch ticking regularly.
  • Moving-coil instruments — galvanometers, ammeters and voltmeters use the proportional twist of a spring.

Key Points

  • Hooke's law: F = kx, valid only within the elastic limit.
  • The spring constant k = F / x measures stiffness; unit N m-1.
  • A load-extension graph is a straight line through the origin within the limit of proportionality.

mcqs.q: A spring balance measures weight or force because:
options: Its spring gets longer as it gets older
The extension of its spring is proportional to the load
Its spring is made of steel
mcqs.why: In a spring balance the extension of the spring is proportional to the load, as Hooke's law states, so equal increases in weight produce equal increases in extension on the scale.

mcqs.q: In vehicle suspension systems and shock absorbers, the springs are chosen according to:
options: Their spring constant, to carry the load smoothly
mcqs.why: Vehicle suspension systems and shock absorbers use springs chosen by their spring constant, so that they compress by the right amount and carry the load smoothly.

mcqs.q: Spring mattresses adjust to the person lying on them because:
options: The springs compress in proportion to the load on them
The springs never compress at all
The springs expand under a load
The springs are equally stiff everywhere in the body
mcqs.why: The springs of a mattress compress in proportion to the load on them, so a heavier part of the body compresses the springs more and the mattress adjusts to the load.

mcqs.q: In a mechanical watch, the spring of the balance wheel is used to:
options: Change the time shown by the hands
mcqs.why: The balance wheel of a mechanical watch depends on its spring obeying Hooke's law, which keeps the watch ticking regularly.

mcqs.q: Galvanometers, ammeters and voltmeters are moving-coil instruments. They work by using:
options: The heating effect of an electric current
The chemical effect of an electric current
The proportional twist of a spring
The expansion of a heated wire
mcqs.why: Moving-coil instruments such as galvanometers, ammeters and voltmeters use the proportional twist of a spring, so the pointer deflection stays proportional to the quantity being measured.

mcqs.q: Hooke's law, on which all these applications depend, is valid:
mcqs.why: Hooke's law, F = k x, is valid only within the elastic limit; beyond that limit the extension is no longer proportional to the force.

mcqs.q: The spring inside a spring balance has a spring constant of 40 N/m. A load stretches it by 0.05 m. The force measured is:
mcqs.why: F = k x = 40 x 0.05 = 2 N. The spring balance turns this proportional extension into a force or weight reading on its scale.

mcqs.q: If a spring balance is loaded beyond the elastic limit of its spring, then:
options: It reads zero for every load
Its readings stay perfectly proportional to the load
Its readings are no longer proportional to the load, because Hooke's law stops holding
mcqs.why: Beyond the elastic limit the extension is no longer proportional to the force, so the evenly spaced scale of the spring balance no longer matches the extension of its spring.

mcqs.q: The spring constant k of a spring is calculated as:
mcqs.why: The spring constant is k = F / x, the ratio of the force to the extension it produces; it measures the stiffness of the spring and its unit is N/m.

mcqs.q: Within the limit of proportionality, the load-extension graph of a spring is:
options: A straight line through the origin
A straight line that does not pass through the origin
mcqs.why: Within the limit of proportionality the load-extension graph is a straight line through the origin, showing that extension is directly proportional to load.

lessons.title: Density
lessons.notes_html:
Density of a substance is its mass per unit volume.

Density = mass / volume

  • ρ (rho) — density
  • m — mass
  • V — volume
  • The SI unit of density is kilogram per cubic metre (kg m-3). Density is also expressed in gram per cubic centimetre (g cm-3), and 1 g cm-3 = 1000 kg m-3.
  • Mass can be found from density: m = ρ × V.

Volumes of Regular Solids

  • Cube of side a: V = a3
  • Sphere of radius r: V = 4/3 π r3
  • Cylinder of radius r and height h: V = π r2 h

Floating and Sinking

  • An object floats on a liquid if its density is less than the density of the liquid.
  • It sinks if its density is greater, and stays suspended inside the liquid if the densities are equal.
  • Ice floats on water because the density of ice (about 0.92 g cm-3) is less than that of water (1.0 g cm-3): on freezing, water expands, so the same mass occupies a larger volume.
  • Iron (about 7.8 g cm-3) sinks in water but floats on mercury (about 13.6 g cm-3).

Worked Example: Density of a Metal

A metallic object of mass 81 g has a volume of 30 cm3. Calculate the density of the object in SI units. Can you identify the metal?

Step 1: Density = mass / volume = 81 / 30 = 2.7 g cm-3.

Step 2: Convert: 2.7 g cm-3 = 2.7 × 1000 = 2700 kg m-3.

Step 3: This is the density of aluminium.

Answer: 2700 kg m-3, aluminium

mcqs.q: Density of a substance is defined as:
options: Its mass multiplied by its volume
mcqs.why: Density = mass / volume: it is the mass contained in one unit volume of the substance, where rho is the density, m is the mass and V is the volume.

mcqs.q: The SI unit of density is:
mcqs.why: The SI unit of density is the kilogram per cubic metre (kg/m^3), because in SI the mass is measured in kilograms and the volume in cubic metres.

mcqs.q: A metallic object of mass 81 g has a volume of 30 cm^3. The density of the object is:
mcqs.why: Density = mass / volume = 81 / 30 = 2.7 g/cm^3. This is the density of aluminium.

mcqs.q: The density 2.7 g/cm^3 expressed in SI units is:
mcqs.why: Since 1 g/cm^3 = 1000 kg/m^3, multiply by 1000: density = 2.7 x 1000 = 2700 kg/m^3.

mcqs.q: The mass of a substance can be found from its density and volume by:
mcqs.why: From density = mass / volume, rearranged: m = rho x V. The mass equals the density multiplied by the volume.

mcqs.q: The volume of a cube of side 2 cm is:
mcqs.why: Volume of a cube = a^3 = 2^3 = 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 cm^3.

mcqs.q: An object floats on a liquid when:
options: Its density is greater than the density of the liquid
Its density is less than the density of the liquid
Its mass is greater than the mass of the liquid
Its volume is less than the volume of the liquid
mcqs.why: An object floats on a liquid if its density is less than the density of the liquid; it sinks if its density is greater, and stays suspended if the densities are equal.

mcqs.q: Ice floats on water because:
options: Water pushes ice upwards like a magnet
The density of ice, about 0.92 g/cm^3, is less than that of water, 1.0 g/cm^3
mcqs.why: On freezing, water expands, so the same mass occupies a larger volume and the density of ice (about 0.92 g/cm^3) becomes less than that of water (1.0 g/cm^3), so ice floats.

mcqs.q: Iron has a density of about 7.8 g/cm^3 and mercury about 13.6 g/cm^3. A piece of iron placed in mercury will:
options: Sink, because iron is a metal
Float, because the density of iron is less than the density of mercury
Stay suspended in the middle of the mercury
mcqs.why: Iron sinks in water because 7.8 g/cm^3 is greater than 1.0 g/cm^3, but it floats on mercury because 7.8 g/cm^3 is less than mercury's 13.6 g/cm^3.

mcqs.q: If an object's density is exactly equal to the density of the liquid it is placed in, the object will:
mcqs.why: When the density of the object equals the density of the liquid, the object neither rises nor sinks: it stays suspended inside the liquid.

lessons.title: Density of Regular and Irregular Solids
lessons.notes_html:
Regularly Shaped Solid

Weigh the solid on a balance to find its mass. Measure its dimensions with a ruler, Vernier callipers or a screw gauge and calculate its volume from the formula for its shape. Then density = mass / volume.

Irregularly Shaped Solid (Displacement Method)

Step 1: Weigh the solid on a balance to find its mass m.

Step 2: Pour water into a measuring cylinder and note the level.

Step 3: Lower the solid fully into the water and note the new level: the rise in level equals the volume V of the solid.

Step 4: Density ρ = m / V.

Worked Example: Mass of an Ice Block

The length, width and height of a rectangular block of ice are 150 cm, 50 cm and 25 cm. If the density of ice is 0.92 g cm-3, calculate the mass of the block in kg.

Step 1: Volume = 150 × 50 × 25 = 187,500 cm3.

Step 2: Mass = density × volume = 0.92 × 187,500 = 172,500 g.

Step 3: Convert: 172,500 g = 172.5 kg.

Answer: 172.5 kg

mcqs.q: To find the density of a regularly shaped solid, its volume is obtained by:
options: Measuring its dimensions and using the formula for its shape
Melting it and pouring it into a measuring cylinder
Weighing it while it is in water
Counting the number of its faces
mcqs.why: For a regular solid, weigh it on a balance to find its mass, measure its dimensions with a ruler, Vernier callipers or a screw gauge, and calculate its volume from the formula for its shape.

mcqs.q: The volume of an irregularly shaped solid is found by:
options: The displacement method: the rise in the water level in a measuring cylinder
Measuring only one side with a ruler
mcqs.why: In the displacement method the solid is lowered fully into water in a measuring cylinder, and the rise in the water level equals the volume of the solid.

mcqs.q: A solid is lowered into a measuring cylinder and the water level rises from 50 cm^3 to 78 cm^3. The volume of the solid is:
mcqs.why: Volume of solid = final level - initial level = 78 - 50 = 28 cm^3. The rise in the water level equals the volume of the solid.

mcqs.q: The solid in the previous measurement has a mass of 224 g. Its density is:
mcqs.why: Density = mass / volume = 224 / 28 = 8 g/cm^3, using the mass from the balance and the volume of 28 cm^3 found by displacement.

mcqs.q: A rectangular block of ice has length 150 cm, width 50 cm and height 25 cm. Its volume is:
mcqs.why: Volume = length x width x height = 150 x 50 x 25 = 187,500 cm^3.

mcqs.q: The density of ice is 0.92 g/cm^3. The mass of the ice block of volume 187,500 cm^3 is:
mcqs.why: Mass = density x volume = 0.92 x 187,500 = 172,500 g. Converting grams to kilograms: 172,500 g = 172.5 kg.

mcqs.q: In the displacement method, the solid must be lowered into the water:
options: Fully, so that it is completely under the water
Only after the water has been removed
mcqs.why: The solid is lowered fully into the water and the new level is noted; only then does the rise in level equal the whole volume of the solid.

mcqs.q: In a density experiment on a solid, its mass is found by using:
mcqs.why: The mass of the solid is found by weighing it on a balance; the measuring cylinder is used to find the volume by displacement, not the mass.

mcqs.q: The correct order of steps for finding the density of an irregular solid is:
options: Find the volume, then guess the mass, then divide
Weigh the solid, note the water level, lower the solid fully, note the new level, then calculate density = m / V
Lower the solid first, then take it out and weigh the water
Measure its sides and use V = a^3
mcqs.why: Step 1: weigh the solid to find its mass m. Step 2: note the water level in the cylinder. Step 3: lower the solid fully and note the new level; the rise gives V. Step 4: density = m / V.

mcqs.q: The dimensions of a regularly shaped solid may be measured with:
options: A ruler, Vernier callipers or a screw gauge
A measuring cylinder and a beaker
A stopwatch and a spring balance
mcqs.why: The dimensions of a regular solid are measured with a ruler, Vernier callipers or a screw gauge, and its volume is then calculated from the formula for its shape.

lessons.title: Density of a Liquid
lessons.notes_html:
To find the density of a liquid: weigh an empty beaker on an electronic balance, pour a measured volume of the liquid into it, and weigh again. The mass of the liquid is the difference of the two readings; density = mass / volume.

Worked Example: Density of Cooking Oil

The mass of an empty beaker is 150.7 g. When 100 ml of cooking oil is poured into the beaker, the balance reads 222.5 g. Calculate the density of cooking oil.

Step 1: Mass of oil = 222.5 - 150.7 = 71.8 g.

Step 2: Volume of oil = 100 ml = 100 cm3.

Step 3: Density = 71.8 / 100 = 0.718 g cm-3 = 718 kg m-3.

Answer: 718 kg m-3

Key Points

  • Density = mass / volume; SI unit kg m-3.
  • Volume: cube a3; sphere 4/3 πr3; cylinder πr2h.
  • The volume of an irregular solid is found by displacement of water.
  • A body floats when its density is less than the liquid's density.

mcqs.q: To find the density of a liquid, the mass of the liquid is obtained by:
options: Weighing the liquid together with the bench
Weighing an empty beaker, then weighing the beaker with the liquid in it, and taking the difference
Estimating it from the volume of the liquid
mcqs.why: Weigh an empty beaker on an electronic balance, pour a measured volume of the liquid into it and weigh again; the mass of the liquid is the difference of the two readings.

mcqs.q: The mass of an empty beaker is 150.7 g. When 100 ml of cooking oil is poured into it, the balance reads 222.5 g. The mass of the oil is:
mcqs.why: Mass of oil = 222.5 - 150.7 = 71.8 g. The mass of the liquid is the difference between the two balance readings.

mcqs.q: The density of that cooking oil (mass 71.8 g, volume 100 ml) is:
mcqs.why: Volume of oil = 100 ml = 100 cm^3. Density = mass / volume = 71.8 / 100 = 0.718 g/cm^3.

mcqs.q: The density of the cooking oil, 0.718 g/cm^3, expressed in SI units is:
mcqs.why: Since 1 g/cm^3 = 1000 kg/m^3, multiply by 1000: 0.718 x 1000 = 718 kg/m^3.

mcqs.q: The empty beaker is weighed before the liquid is poured in so that:
options: The volume of the beaker can be measured
The beaker can be cooled down
The mass of the beaker can be subtracted, leaving only the mass of the liquid
The balance can be switched on
mcqs.why: The mass of the liquid is the difference of the two readings, so the mass of the empty beaker must be known first and subtracted from the combined reading.

mcqs.q: In the liquid-density method, the volume of liquid used must be:
options: Guessed from the colour of the liquid
Calculated from the mass of the liquid
mcqs.why: A measured volume of the liquid is poured into the beaker; the density is then found as the mass of the liquid divided by this measured volume.

mcqs.q: A liquid of mass 45 g occupies a volume of 50 cm^3. Its density is:
mcqs.why: Density = mass / volume = 45 / 50 = 0.9 g/cm^3.

mcqs.q: In the method described for finding the density of a liquid, the beaker is weighed on:
options: A spring balance hanging from a stand
A balance that only reads in kilograms
mcqs.why: The method uses an electronic balance: the empty beaker is weighed on it, the liquid is added, and it is weighed again so the mass of the liquid is found by difference.

mcqs.q: When the density of a liquid is reported in SI units, the unit used is:
mcqs.why: Density = mass / volume and its SI unit is the kilogram per cubic metre (kg/m^3); a value in g/cm^3 is multiplied by 1000 to convert it to kg/m^3.

mcqs.q: Cooking oil has a density of 0.718 g/cm^3 and water has a density of 1.0 g/cm^3. Poured into water, the oil will:
options: Sink, because its density is smaller
Float on the water, because its density is less than the density of water
Stay suspended in the middle of the water
mcqs.why: A body floats on a liquid when its density is less than the density of the liquid: 0.718 g/cm^3 is less than 1.0 g/cm^3, so the oil floats on water.

lessons.title: Introduction and the Particle Theory
lessons.notes_html:
Introduction

Matter consists of extremely small particles called atoms, molecules or ions, and these particles are not visible to the naked eye. One or more atoms of the same or different elements combine to form a molecule. Matter exists in three states: solid, liquid and gas, and it can change its state on heating or cooling. For example, ice (the solid form of water) converts into water on heating, and further heating converts water into steam, its gaseous form; on cooling, steam changes back into water and then into ice. Pressure can also change the state of matter: gases can be liquefied under high pressure. The existence of the three states may be explained on the basis of the particle theory of matter.

Particle Theory of Matter

The particle theory of matter is based on the following postulates:

  • (a) Matter consists of extremely small particles. These particles are atoms, molecules or ions.
  • (b) Particles are in constant motion and thus possess kinetic energy. The motion of particles can be translational, vibrational or rotational, or a combination of these; the nature of the motion depends on the state of matter.
  • (c) The particles of matter attract each other, and this force depends on the separation between the particles: the smaller the separation between the particles, the greater the force of attraction between them.

mcqs.q: According to the particle theory, matter consists of:
options: Extremely small particles called atoms, molecules or ions
Large pieces that are visible to the naked eye
A continuous sheet with no particles in it
mcqs.why: Matter consists of extremely small particles called atoms, molecules or ions, and these particles are not visible to the naked eye.

mcqs.q: A molecule is formed when:
options: A gas is compressed in a cylinder
One or more atoms of the same or different elements combine
mcqs.why: One or more atoms of the same or different elements combine to form a molecule.

mcqs.q: The three states of matter are:
mcqs.why: Matter exists in three states: solid, liquid and gas, and it can change its state on heating or cooling.

mcqs.q: On heating, ice changes into water. On further heating, the water changes into:
mcqs.why: Ice, the solid form of water, converts into water on heating, and further heating converts water into steam, its gaseous form; on cooling, steam changes back into water and then into ice.

mcqs.q: Gases can be liquefied by:
options: Leaving them in the open air
Adding more gas to the container
mcqs.why: Pressure can also change the state of matter: gases can be liquefied under high pressure.

mcqs.q: Which statement is a postulate of the particle theory of matter?
options: Particles of matter are at rest and have no energy
Particles repel each other at every distance
Particles can be seen with the naked eye
Particles are in constant motion and thus possess kinetic energy
mcqs.why: Postulate (b) of the particle theory: the particles are in constant motion and thus possess kinetic energy; the motion can be translational, vibrational or rotational, depending on the state of matter.

mcqs.q: The motion of the particles of matter can be:
options: Translational, vibrational or rotational, or a combination of these
